# Dan's Motorcycle "Motorcycle Carburetor Repair "

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carbs.htm

CARBURETORS

![064_slide_carb_cv_carburetors_slide_carb.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_slide_carb_cv_carburetors_slide_carb.jpg>)

"Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire devoureth both the ends of it,
and the midst of it is burned. Is it meet for any work?"
Ezekiel 15:4

¶ Without fuel for the fire that motorcycle engine will simply not be "meet

![064_meet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_meet.jpg>)

for any work".

First things first. Go get a working fire extinguisher and put it in easy reach. Like right beside the bike you are working on. Trust me... if you work on carburetors and engines long enough you will light yourself,
or an engine, off sooner or later.

Play it safe and have a fire extinguisher close by...
If you don't... It is OK... I DON'T CARE!
IT'S NOT MY BODY AND IT WON'T HURT ME AT ALL!

![064_s_not_my_body_won_t_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_s_not_my_body_won_t_2.jpg>)

![064_s_not_my_body_won_t.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_s_not_my_body_won_t.jpg>)

Dirty Carburetor

![064_dirty_carburetor_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_dirty_carburetor_2.jpg>)

![064_dirty_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_dirty_carburetor.jpg>)

Exploded Carburetor

![064_dirty_carburetor_exploded_carburetor_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_dirty_carburetor_exploded_carburetor_2.jpg>)

![064_dirty_carburetor_exploded_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_dirty_carburetor_exploded_carburetor.jpg>)

Dirty Carburetor

Most carburetor problems seem to come, as you might guess, after the machine has set idle for a while. The real cure is to use Gasoline Stabilizer in your gas whenever the bike is going to sit, unused, for a long period of time. However it happens, if you have compression and spark but it still won't start. If the engine only runs with the choke on or the enrichening lever pulled out,
you have one or more jets plugged. Notice I said enrichening lever... most of the motorcycle carbs have enrichening passages

![064_enrichening_passages.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_enrichening_passages.jpg>)

inside the carburetor that,
WHEN THE THROTTLE IS CLOSED, provide the rich air/fuel mixture to start the engine. If you open the throttle any at all it cuts this enrichening out of the system.
So if you are having trouble starting, and everything looks ok, see if closing the throttle helps. This does not apply to carburetors with
a butterfly choke

![064_butterfly_choke.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_butterfly_choke.jpg>)

.

![064_does_not_apply_carburetors_butterfly_choke_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_does_not_apply_carburetors_butterfly_choke_2.jpg>)

![064_does_not_apply_carburetors_butterfly_choke.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_does_not_apply_carburetors_butterfly_choke.jpg>)

To get to the jets you will have to take the carburetor(s) off the engine. A shop manual will be very helpful here for float settings and exploded pictures of the
carburetor

![064_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_carburetor.jpg>)

. Use some Gunk engine cleaner and clean off the entire engine and carburetors before you start. After you get the carburetor(s) off, if necessary get some solvent and clean again the outside of the carburetors. DO NOT go ripping everything down to individual parts. Work smart, not hard. If you take everything apart you risk breaking or losing things that are not broken and that are working just fine. POW, there goes a spring you thought you had a hold of. It is in orbit now and you will never see it again. Then you find out it is not available, except on Ebay in a complete four carburetor assembly for $500 and no, they will not sell it alone.

![064_carburetor_assembly.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_carburetor_assembly.jpg>)

![064_then_find_out_not_available_except.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_then_find_out_not_available_except.jpg>)

Multiple carburetors are normally bolted together as an assembly. This makes the connections between the carburetors very stable. That in turn allows easy adjustment of the throttle slides so each slide opens and closes the same as all the others. If you take everything apart the adjustments will be lost. These settings are pretty stable and only change after many miles of wear. Remember you are not replacing worn out parts. You are fixing plugged up parts. Yes, some of the parts will be worn like the Fuel Inlet Needle and Seat but most parts are just plugged and/or dirty. I like to take a tray, one for each carburetor, number the trays, and then put the parts from each carburetor in it's own tray. That way you don't mix up the parts from each carburetor with parts from another.

I like to take the top off the carburetor(s) and look at the slide and jet needle first. Usually the slide and Diaphragm are not too bad. I check for holes in the Diaphragm and clean the slide with a shop rag with some spray carburetor cleaner on it. Be careful not to get any cleaner on the rubber Diaphragm.

![064_careful_not_get_any_cleaner_rubber_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_careful_not_get_any_cleaner_rubber_2.jpg>)

![064_careful_not_get_any_cleaner_rubber.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_careful_not_get_any_cleaner_rubber.jpg>)

Now take the float bowl(s) off and remove the jets. Sounds so easy doesn't it? Sometimes it is, and other times it's a mass of gook.
If it is, scrape as much of the gook out as possible, and boil out the rest with carb cleaner. Now don't throw the whole thing in the cleaner, Look at it first.
Does it have rubber seals

![064_careful_not_get_any_cleaner_rubber.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_careful_not_get_any_cleaner_rubber.jpg>)

on the throttle shafts? Look close... sometimes these seals are hard to see and are not shown in the parts books, meaning you can't get them so you do not want to ruin them.
If they are there and you can't get them you will have to scrape and clean the carb body carefully by hand and not soak it. Use a small wire brush, a small screwdiver and some spray carburetor cleaner. Keep at it and sooner or later you will get it clean.

Again, for these reasons most multi carburetor assemblies do not and should not be completely disassembled and dumped into carburetor cleaner. Just disassemble them far enough to do a good cleaning job.

![064_just_disassemble_them_far_enough_do_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_just_disassemble_them_far_enough_do_2.jpg>)

![064_just_disassemble_them_far_enough_do.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_just_disassemble_them_far_enough_do.jpg>)

Before you remove the air screw, turn it in till it bottoms, counting the turns. When you replace it, set it at this setting to start. there are many different styles of air screws.

![064_just_disassemble_them_far_enough_do.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_just_disassemble_them_far_enough_do.jpg>)

Sometimes there is a rubber o-ring and steel washer under the air screw spring and sometimes not.
Look for it and if there is one, dig it out with a needle BEFORE you spray carburetor cleaner in there. The air screw may be covered by a plug similar to this one.

![064_air_screw_may_covered_plug_similar.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_air_screw_may_covered_plug_similar.jpg>)

You will have to remove this plug to get to it.
I usually set the air screw about 1 & 1/4 turns out, if I don't have a setting. When the engine is warm, turn the screw in till the engine stumbles, then out till it stumbles, and leave it at half way in between.
Adjust the idle with the throttle stop screw as needed.

Throttle adjustment screws

![064_throttle_adjustment_screws.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_throttle_adjustment_screws.jpg>)

, sometimes called the throttle stop screw, are normally located at the center of the carburetor on most single cylinder motorcycles. Multi cylinder motorcycles have numerous ways of adjusting the throttle and are usually adjusted on the side of one the carburetors

![064_one_carburetors.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_one_carburetors.jpg>)

and sometimes in the center between the carburetors.

![064_center_between_carburetors.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_center_between_carburetors.jpg>)

You will need to remove the Main jet and the Needle jet. The Main jet

![064_main_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_main_jet.jpg>)

is usually screwed on to the lower end of the Needle jet, locking it into the carb. Remove the main jet and tap out the needle jet.

![064_needle_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_needle_jet.jpg>)

Do this very carefully. It can break very easily. Sometimes the needle jet will have an O-ring. Remove the O-ring and soak both main jet and needle jet in carburetor cleaner. When you put it back in, there is a pin in the carb body that fits in a grove on the needle jet. Make sure they match up.

Be careful not to strip or break the small idle jet when you try to remove it. It may be necessary to grind the end of a small screwdriver to fit the jet just right. Be aware that some idle jets are pressed in

![064_pressed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_pressed.jpg>)

and cannot be removed.

![064_aware_some_idle_jets_pressed_cannot_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_aware_some_idle_jets_pressed_cannot_2.jpg>)

![064_aware_some_idle_jets_pressed_cannot.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_aware_some_idle_jets_pressed_cannot.jpg>)

Even after soaking, the jet may still be plugged. If so take one wire

![064_aware_some_idle_jets_pressed_cannot.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_aware_some_idle_jets_pressed_cannot.jpg>)

out of a wire brush and gently push it threw the jet. The wire brush shown has wires that are
.013" in diameter. The smallest jet drill you can get is a #80, which has a diameter of .0135". So you can use the wire and not enlarge the hole, at least not by much. Yes, I know all the books say not to use anything to
clean out the jet hole. However, they live in a world where you can always get a new jet easily and cheaply. This is not the world I live in. Be sure that you can see light, or squirt carburetor cleaner, through each jet. If you can't, it is still plugged.

Compressed air works good too, only hold the jet in a shop rag so you do not give yourself an air embolism. I usually squirt some spray can carb cleaner into the carb passages, then blow it through with compressed air.
I then look down the throat of the carburetor, as I blow it out, and make sure it comes out where it is supposed to come out, and that those small idle passages are clear. Wear goggles

![064_wear_goggles.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_wear_goggles.jpg>)

and don't get so close that you get that stuff in your eyes.

![064_wear_goggles_don_t_get_so_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_wear_goggles_don_t_get_so_2.jpg>)

![064_wear_goggles_don_t_get_so.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_wear_goggles_don_t_get_so.jpg>)

Sometimes the shafts that hold the carburetor floats can be badly gooked up or rusted. Use a penetrating oil of some kind and let it set awhile. By awhile I mean several hours, maybe overnight. It took many months for it to get gooked up. Seems only right it should take some time to remedy it. The oil will loosen up the parts so that you can drive out the pin with a very small
punch. If necessary, tap on the punch very, very gently. The posts that hold the floats are very weak and break easily. Carburetor bodies can be very costly to replace! If necessary make supports

![064_wear_goggles_don_t_get_so.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_wear_goggles_don_t_get_so.jpg>)

to back up the posts. Also the float pin may (or may not) be serrated on one end

![064_serrated_one_end.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_serrated_one_end.jpg>)

so you have to pull the pin out from the serrated end. The serrated end cuts into the float support, locking it in.

Spray penetrating oil also works good to free up stuck throttle slides too. If the slides have a rubber diaphragm

![064_rubber_diaphragm.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_rubber_diaphragm.jpg>)

on them, spray carburetor cleaner on a rag and wipe the slide clean. Do not get any carb cleaner on the Diaphragm. It will ruin it. While you have the Diaphragm out inspect it for holes

![064_holes.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_holes.jpg>)

. If you have an engine that has good compression, starts well, but just has no power and revs up, ever so slowly... check that rubber diaphragm... I'll bet it has a hole in it.

When you put the fuel inlet needle back in, put one drop of light oil on it so it will move freely in it's seat and not stick before the gas first starts to fill the bowl.

Don't clean the outside of constant velocity carburetors with spray carburetor cleaner unless you are sure they are not the Rubber Diaphragm type

![064_rubber_diaphragm_type.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_rubber_diaphragm_type.jpg>)

...
the cleaner will eat the rubber. There is an all steel piston type

![064_piston_type.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_piston_type.jpg>)

of CV carburetor but it's still not a good idea to use the spray because of rubber float bowl gaskets. Notice too, the top seal is a Labyrinth seal.

![064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal_2.jpg>)

![064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal.jpg>)

![064_needle_seat.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_needle_seat.gif>)

![064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal.gif>)

If you turn on the fuel petcock and gas pours out the overflow tube, tap lightly on the carburetor body with a plastic hammer(or something like it). That will jiggle the fuel inlet needle loose.
Same thing if there is dirt holding the needle open. If it doesn't work you need a new needle & seat

![064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_notice_too_top_seal_labyrinth_seal.jpg>)

. The tips of the fuel inlet needle can be either steel or rubber. Tips with a groove worn in them

![064_groove_worn_them.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_groove_worn_them.jpg>)

should be replaced.

Floats control how much gas there is in the float bowl. The Tang

![064_tang.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_tang.jpg>)

of the float presses on the float needle (fuel inlet needle) letting gas into the float chamber when the level is low and shutting it off when it gets too high. If the Tang is metal, you can adjust the float level by bending it up or down. If it is plastic,

![064_plastic.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_plastic.jpg>)

it is normally not adjustable. Sometimes, you may run across a plastic float that has a metal insert

![064_plastic_float_has_metal_insert.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_plastic_float_has_metal_insert.jpg>)

that is adjustable.

![064_sometimes_may_run_across_plastic_float.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_sometimes_may_run_across_plastic_float.jpg>)

![064_tang.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_tang.jpg>)

Float levels

![064_tang.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_tang.jpg>)

are different for each bike and are found in the bikes shop manual. If you don't have the float setting and can't find it anywhere, set it so the fuel level is a bit below the top of the float bowl. Make sure no gas comes out of the Float Over Flow

![064_over_flow.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_over_flow.jpg>)

Tube/Hose. The Float Over Flow Tube is at the bottom of each carburetor. That should get you in the ballpark. Adjust the fuel level down from there as needed.

There are many styles of floats

![064_floats.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_floats.jpg>)

. If you have Copper Floats, and the bike has been sitting out in the cold, with the temperature down below freezing, it's possible for water to get into the carb and freeze. This can crush the floats

![064_crush_floats.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_crush_floats.jpg>)

and make the carburetor overflow, when you turn on the gas in the spring. Too high of fuel level can cause the carbs to leak too.

Part of the enrichening circuit is in the main carburetor body

![064_carburetor_body.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_carburetor_body.jpg>)

and part is in the float bowl

![064_float_bowl.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_float_bowl.jpg>)

. The Enrichening Plunger

![064_enrichening_plunger.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_enrichening_plunger.jpg>)

basically, when it is raised, uncovers a passageway to a very small cast in jet in the float bowl. This little jet can get plugged so when you clean the float bowl, make sure it is clear. I like to put some spray carburetor cleaner down the large passageway and see if it comes out the lower hole

![064_lower_hole.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_lower_hole.jpg>)

. Remember, don't get your eyes too close and "Goggles

![064_wear_goggles.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_wear_goggles.jpg>)

are your friend." The jet is cast into the lower part of the passageway, hard to see and not removable on most carburetors but not all. Sometimes they are screwed in.

![064_screwed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_screwed.jpg>)

Sometimes the jet is in a tube

![064_tube.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_tube.jpg>)

that sticks into the Float Bowl. If it is plugged, the choke will not work.

If the rubber boots and tubes, that connect the carburetor and the air cleaner housing, are old and hard, you should get new ones. However, sometimes they are not available. Try soaking them in carb cleaner. Soaking them will make them soft and pliable.
You can soak them from several minutes to twenty minutes or more. Keep checking them till they look and feel right. Too long and it will ruin them. Of course, they are already junk anyway! You can also heat them in boiling water.
This works real good, but they harden up real quick when they cool, so work fast. Because of old, hard rubber manifolds and tubes you may have to lever and pry the carburetors off. Be very careful when you do this. Carburetors are pot metal, very weak and easy to break. Lubing things up with Armor All and warming things up gently with a hot air gun can help.

![064_lubing_things_up_armor_all_warming_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_lubing_things_up_armor_all_warming_2.jpg>)

![064_lubing_things_up_armor_all_warming.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_lubing_things_up_armor_all_warming.jpg>)

You can sometimes rejuvenate a rubber part by soaking it in Armor All for a day or two. This seems to help the rubber tips

![064_lubing_things_up_armor_all_warming.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_lubing_things_up_armor_all_warming.jpg>)

of some fuel inlet needles, provided they are in pretty good condition to start with.
You can squirt Armor All on the insides of the air box tubes to help them slip onto the carburetors too.

On the side of some carburetors there is another diaphragm

![064_diaphragm.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_diaphragm.jpg>)

that temporarily closes the slow speed jet air passage when the throttle is closed. This richens the fuel mixture, to reduce backfiring, when coming to a stop. Check it for holes and hope you don't have any. They are quite pricey.

At the bottom of some carbs is an accelerator pump

![064_accelerator_pump.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_accelerator_pump.jpg>)

, to pump extra fuel

![064_extra_fuel.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_extra_fuel.jpg>)

when the throttle is opened. On multi-cylinder bikes usually only one carburetor has a pump and it is connected to the throats of the other carburetors by passages or tubing.
Check this Diaphragm, also, for holes or cracks.

All new Diaphragms can be expensive and hard to get. I have heard of people using a spray on rubber coating called " Plasti Dip " to fix diaphragms. I have never used it but I hear it works. Get it from NAPA part # 765-2527. Worth a try anyway.

The throttle slide can go in backwards...this jams the throttle wide open... Not Good...make sure it goes in the right way.

![064_make_sure_goes_right_way_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_make_sure_goes_right_way_2.jpg>)

![064_make_sure_goes_right_way.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_make_sure_goes_right_way.jpg>)

There are only two adjustments that you can make from outside the carburetor. The idle screw (Throttle stop screw) adjusts the speed of the idle. The idle air screw adjusts the idle mixture. This is only at idle and does not effect anything above idle. Here is another method to adjust it. Screw the air screw in and out until you get the highest idle speed. Then lower the idle speed with the idle screw and do it again until you get the best idle. The air screw can be located on the right or left side of the carburetor. It can also be on the top or bottom, in the front of the carburetor too! To top it off, if you have a 1980 or newer machine, it may have a cover

![064_make_sure_goes_right_way.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_make_sure_goes_right_way.jpg>)

over it to keep you from messing with it. You will have to drill or pry it out somehow. EasyOuts work good for this. Watch out, it may be illegal for you to do this, depending on where you live and whether this is a racing motorcycle or not.

If you can't get it to idle, or rather the idle stays real high then drops off and dies, check for an air leak at the carburetor manifold. Squirt some gas or starting fluid on the manifold and see if the revs change. If they do, you have a leak.
If your valves clearances are too tight, it will also effect the idle.

You can make your air /fuel mixture a bit richer or leaner by moving the carburetor needle clip

![064_carburetor_needle_clip.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_carburetor_needle_clip.jpg>)

up or down. Move the clip down a notch to raise the needle, to richen the mixture. Move the clip up to lower the needle, to lean out the mixture. The needle is located in the throttle slide.

![064_throttle_slide.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_throttle_slide.jpg>)

![064_needle_located_throttle_slide_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_needle_located_throttle_slide_2.jpg>)

![064_needle_located_throttle_slide.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_needle_located_throttle_slide.jpg>)

You should always turn the fuel off. If you don't and the carb inlet needle fails, it will fill your crankcase full of gas. Not good. If you have a four stroke, it thins out the oil and parts start to weld together... really not good. If you have a two stroke it will fill up the crankcase with fuel and can cause it to hydraulically lock. But at least it will not overheat the engine. A lot of newer bikes have a fuel petcock

![064_needle_located_throttle_slide.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_needle_located_throttle_slide.jpg>)

with a Diaphragm that only lets fuel into the carb if the engine is running. It operates on vacuum pressure. Normally you have three settings. On, reserve, and Prime. Prime bypasses the diaphragm to let fuel into the carburetor after it has set a long time.

Finally, a word on parts. Use only the carburetors manufacturers brand of parts. Such as Mikuni, Keihin, Bing, Amal, ETC. Do Not use aftermarket carburetor kits or parts. Their quality control is lousy (all of them!) Trust me on this, I speak from way too much experience. I have installed no less then sixteen aftermarket carburetor kits and there will not be a seventeenth. Yes, you are right I am a slow learner (But man, the kits are so cheap!). Oh, how many hours did I waste figuring out which "New" jets were bad? I don't even like to think.

How do you tell if a jet is Genuine Keihin or Mikuni or Bing or Amal or whatever? Simple, each jet will be marked with the Logo of the manufacturer. A "K" for Keihin or a "square within a square" for Mikuni. Bing has a "B", Amal has, well. "AMAL" and so on an so forth. I think you get the Idea. They are proud of their parts. If there is no name... how proud is that?

![064_how_proud_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_how_proud_2.jpg>)

![064_how_proud.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_how_proud.jpg>)

Keihin Logo

![064_keihin_logo_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo_2.jpg>)

![064_keihin_logo.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo.jpg>)

Mikuni Logo

![064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_2.jpg>)

![064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo.jpg>)

Bing Logo

![064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_bing_logo_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_bing_logo_2.jpg>)

![064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_bing_logo.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_bing_logo.jpg>)

Amal Logo

Keep your Carburetors clean and they will be "meet

![064_meet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_meet.jpg>)

for any work".

![064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_bing_logo_2.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/064_keihin_logo_mikuni_logo_bing_logo_2.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle Carburator Balancing

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/balancecarbs.htm

BALANCING CARBURATORS

![065_balancing_carburators_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_balancing_carburators_2.jpg>)

![065_balancing_carburators.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_balancing_carburators.jpg>)

Let me be weighed in an even balance that God may know mine integrity.
Job 31:6

![065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor_3.jpg>)

![065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor.jpg>)

![065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor_4.jpg>)

![065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor_2.jpg>)

If you have more than one carburetor you want them to have an even balance. If they are out of balance the cylinders fight each other causing vibration.
No Balance equals no Integrity.

The best way to balance your carburetors is with some form of Mercury Manometer.

![065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_have_more_than_one_carburetor.jpg>)

The manometer measures intake manifold vacuum pressure. You want the pressure to be the same in all of the carburetor manifolds.
In the carburetor manifolds, or on the front of the carburetors themselves, you will find small tubes that you can push a rubber hose over, or little threaded holes that you can thread a fitting into. You attach the hoses from the Manometer to these tubes or fittings.

![065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_3.jpg>)

![065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings.jpg>)

![065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_4.jpg>)

![065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_2.jpg>)

With the fittings attached

![065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings.jpg>)

and the Manometer connected, start the engine. It is a good idea to have a large fan blowing on the engine to help cool it. With the engine warm, adjust all carburetors to read about the same manifold pressure. Normally, this is within 2 cm Hg of each other. Just get all the carburetors reading within 2 cm of each other. The Manometers are marked in 2 cm increments. Usually there are only three screws to mess with. You match

![065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_attach_hoses_manometer_these_tubes_fittings_2.jpg>)

carburetors 1 and 2 to each other, then 3 and 4 to each other, then match carburetors banks 1/2 and 3/4 to each other. When you are finished, blip the throttle several times and let the throttle snap shut each time. Now check and make sure all the cylinders are still matched. If you wanted to do this several times, it would not hurt!

![065_if_wanted_do_several_times_would_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_wanted_do_several_times_would_2.jpg>)

![065_if_wanted_do_several_times_would.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_if_wanted_do_several_times_would.jpg>)

One Cylinder out of Sync

![065_one_cylinder_out_sync_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_one_cylinder_out_sync_2.jpg>)

![065_one_cylinder_out_sync.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_one_cylinder_out_sync.jpg>)

All Carburetors are in Sync

![065_one_cylinder_out_sync_all_carburetors_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_one_cylinder_out_sync_all_carburetors_2.jpg>)

![065_one_cylinder_out_sync_all_carburetors.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_one_cylinder_out_sync_all_carburetors.jpg>)

Carburetor Banks 1 & 2
out of Sync

The adjusting screws

![065_adjusting_screws.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_adjusting_screws.jpg>)

are between the carburetors and hard to get to unless you have a Special Tool.

![065_special_tool.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_special_tool.jpg>)

Some carburetors

![065_carburetors.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_carburetors.jpg>)

do not require a special tool and can be adjusted with just a long screw driver. You have to work fast. Once the engine gets too hot, it will be hard to get good readings. If this happens, stop the engine, let it cool down then re-test. As always, a shop manual is very helpful.

![065_always_shop_manual_very_helpful_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_always_shop_manual_very_helpful_2.jpg>)

![065_always_shop_manual_very_helpful.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_always_shop_manual_very_helpful.jpg>)

Carburetor Tool in use

![065_carburetor_tool_use_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_carburetor_tool_use_2.jpg>)

![065_carburetor_tool_use.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_carburetor_tool_use.jpg>)

Carburetor Tool Tip

You really must have the Manometer if you have CV type carburetors. However, I have noticed that if the CV carburetors are in balance, the engine will rev up smoothly with no stumbling, when you whack the throttle open hard, from an idle, with the engine in neutral. If it stumbles, they are probably out of balance. Be careful and don't over-rev the engine. If you do this with an engine that has normal slide carburetors, the engine will die. This is normal. With too big of throttle opening at idle the vacuum disappears. With no vacuum, no gas is sucked from the carburetor. No gas... No run!

![065_no_run_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_no_run_3.jpg>)

![065_no_run.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_no_run.jpg>)

![065_no_run_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_no_run_4.jpg>)

![065_no_run_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_no_run_2.jpg>)

Speaking of gas. Many machines have a fuel petcock that is vacuum operated. Honda says "If the motorcycle is equipped with an automatic fuel valve, disconnect the vacuum tube from the intake manifold of the carburetor, draw vacuum and pinch the tube with a clip

![065_no_run.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_no_run.jpg>)

as shown." However, they don't bother to mention that you better plug that hole in the intake manifold or you will get some funny readings off that carburetor. I prefer to remove the gas tank and, after pugging that manifold hole, use a remote gas tank to feed fuel to all the carburetors while you perform the balancing tests. I use an old lawn mower gas tank

![065_no_run_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_no_run_2.jpg>)

but any tank with a hose will do. Just make sure the tank is made to hold gas. Milk jugs and things like that will fail and create a big time fire hazard.

Some carburetors have no Manometer fittings. If you have one of these, you will have to invent a way to make sure the throttle slides rise and fall together.

Take the air cleaner off and stick your fingers in two of the carburetors and feel the slides move (Engine off, I would hope!).
Listen to the slides hit the throttle stops.
Look at them. See which throttle slides move first.
Put pencils under the slides and see if all the pencils move the same as the throttle opens.

![065_balancer.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_balancer.jpg>)

![065_put_pencils_under_slides_see_if.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_put_pencils_under_slides_see_if.jpg>)

Lots of funny ways to do it. Maybe even try looking in the shop manual! If the carburetors are normal slide carburetors, that is, with a solid connection between the throttle cable and the throttle slide, you don't absolutely have to have a Mammometer... but it sure helps. They do make a Manometer

![065_put_pencils_under_slides_see_if.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_put_pencils_under_slides_see_if.jpg>)

that fits on the carburetor bell, but I'm not impressed with the one I have.

I prefer to use a mercury manometer. The reason they use mercury is because it is very heavy and usually will not be sucked into the engine. I have heard of that happening but it has never happened to me. It also helps dampen the intake pulses. If you run a search on the Internet you will find lots of plans for Manometers using different weight oils and the like. I have never tried to make one but I see no reason why you could not. You may have to put some kind of restrictors in the lines to the carburetors to dampen out the intake pulses. I have seen people use a set of vacuum gauges with success too.

![065_mammometer.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_mammometer.gif>)

![065_i_have_seen_people_use_set.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_i_have_seen_people_use_set.jpg>)

I am surprised at the amount of E-Mail about my little Mammometer typo! I think I shall leave it just because it seems to bother so many men. Strange, no women have complained... only men! I mean really guys, it does kind of look like the right tool, doesn't it! But I don't want to disappoint anyone so here

![065_but_i_don_t_want_disappoint.pdf](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_but_i_don_t_want_disappoint.pdf>)

is a PDF file of a patent for a real Mammometer. There you go guys... have at it!

![001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg>)

![065_have.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/065_have.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle "Idle Circuit"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb3.htm

The Idle Circuit

![067_idle_circuit_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_circuit_2.jpg>)

![067_idle_circuit.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_circuit.jpg>)

"But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak,
they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment."
Matthew 12:36

¶ Idle words seem to abound these days, especially in Government circles. I think they all are in for a big fatal surprise. Lots of Idle words are spoken about Carburetors too. People say just change this jet or that jet and boom, you get lots more horsepower and 100 miles per gallon. People believe this because there are so many different Jets available. In addition they are relatively cheap and easy to get to so people figure, "Why Not Change something." Motorcycle Factories spend many hours and lots of money to get the carburetion just right. Then "We the People" come along and try to make things better. We usually end up with a bike that does not run as good as it did before we started. However, not always. We should leave well enough alone but you are going to do it anyway, aren't you?

In an effort to help you do this, and avoid that surprise, I will now bloviate about the different circuits in the Carburetor. I will cover Mechanical Slide Carburetors first. We will start with Idle Circuits.

The Idle Circuit controls the engine speed from Idle to about one quarter throttle. Humm, I guess that covers it... or maybe not! Things are a bit more complicated then what it might first seem. The Idle Circuit has an Idle jet, a screw that adjusts it and an idle stop screw of some kind to adjust the Engine Idle Speed. You set the Idle Adjuster Screw one and a half turns out from bottom. Then start the engine, let it get warm and adjust the Idle Speed with the Throttle Stop Screw till you get the lowest idle. Then turn the Idle Adjuster Screw in or out till you get the best idle. Then do it all again until you get the smoothest Idle at the idle speed you want.

![067_then_do_all_again_until_get_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_then_do_all_again_until_get_2.jpg>)

![067_then_do_all_again_until_get.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_then_do_all_again_until_get.jpg>)

Throttle Closed

![067_throttle_closed_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_throttle_closed_2.jpg>)

![067_throttle_closed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_throttle_closed.jpg>)

Throttle Quarter Open

As you can see above, there is a small Idle Port in the throat of the Carburetor. This port is controlled by the Idle Adjuster Screw. As the throttle opens, The Throttle Slide uncovers another Idle Port. This second port has a straight shot from the Idle Jet to the throat of the Carburetor. This helps smooth the transition to the next Carburetor Circuit. Most Throttle Slide Carburetors have these two ports. Some Carburetors have three Idle Ports

![067_three_idle_ports.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_three_idle_ports.jpg>)

. I have only seen three ports on Constant Velocity type Carburetors. Most Idle Jets Screw in to the Carburetor. Unfortunately, I'm starting to see Idle Jets that are pressed in

![067_pressed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_pressed.jpg>)

and are not replaceable in some of the newer Carburetors.

![067_unfortunately_i_m_starting_see_idle_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_unfortunately_i_m_starting_see_idle_2.jpg>)

![067_unfortunately_i_m_starting_see_idle.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_unfortunately_i_m_starting_see_idle.jpg>)

Idle Jet Installed

![067_idle_jet_installed_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_jet_installed_2.jpg>)

![067_idle_jet_installed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_jet_installed.jpg>)

Idle Jet Out

![067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out_3.jpg>)

![067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out.jpg>)

Idle Jet Seat

![067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out_4.jpg>)

![067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_idle_jet_installed_idle_jet_out_2.jpg>)

Idle Jet Seat
with my
trusty Microscope

Now there are two ways the fuel mixture is mixed before it leaves the idle ports and goes into the engine. In the first and most common way, air is taken from the front, air cleaner side, of the carburetor. Sometimes called the Carburetor Bell. Then the air is mixed with the fuel from the Idle Jet. It then goes out through the idle port(s). In other words, the amount of air in the air/fuel mix is adjusted by the Idle Adjustment Screw. This type of Idle Adjustment is used on Carburetors that go on both Two-Stroke and Four-Stroke engines.

![067_type_idle_adjustment_used_carburetors_go_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_type_idle_adjustment_used_carburetors_go_2.jpg>)

![067_type_idle_adjustment_used_carburetors_go.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_type_idle_adjustment_used_carburetors_go.jpg>)

Air Adjust Idle Screw 1

![067_air_adjust_idle_screw_1_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_air_adjust_idle_screw_1_2.jpg>)

![067_air_adjust_idle_screw_1.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_air_adjust_idle_screw_1.jpg>)

Air Adjust Idle Screw 2

The second way is for fuel to be taken from the Idle Jet and channeled directly into the Idle Port, in front of the Carburetor Slide, on the engine side of the Carburetor. Here, the Idle Jet Adjuster Screw controls the amount of fuel that is introduced to the Carburetor Venturi. Some people have called Carburetors that use this type of Idle Jet adjustment "Four-Stroke Carburetors". While I have never seen a Two-Stroke engine use this type of Carburetor, I see no reason why you could not use one on a Two-Stroke.

![067_while_i_have_never_seen_two_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_while_i_have_never_seen_two_2.jpg>)

![067_while_i_have_never_seen_two.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_while_i_have_never_seen_two.jpg>)

Fuel Adjust Idle Screw 1

![067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_2.jpg>)

![067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1.jpg>)

Fuel Adjust Idle Screw 2

![067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel_3.jpg>)

![067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel.jpg>)

Air Adjust and
Fuel Adjust Idle Screws

![067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel_4.jpg>)

![067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_fuel_adjust_idle_screw_1_fuel_2.jpg>)

Sectioned Idle Jet
About 3/4"/ 19 mm long
That is one little, tiny, jet!

The best Air/Fuel Ratio, for a motorcycle engine, is around 14.7 parts air to one part fuel. The adjuster screws reflect this. If you look at the Air Adjuster screw you will see it is a lot more gross than the Fuel Adjuster Screw which is a lot more precise.

You probably will not need to change the Idle Jet much. If you do want to change the Idle Jet you are in luck. (????) There are dozens of Idle Jet sizes. You will need to change the Idle Jet to the desired size. Adjust the Idle Screw and set the idle speed. Then take a new or cleaned spark plug and put it in the engine. Run the engine at an idle long enough to color the plug. Don't overheat the engine. You want a good idle, a smooth transition past quarter throttle and good spark plug color. Don't like the color of the spark plug? Can't get it to idle good? Pick a different Idle Jet and do it all over again.

§ On to Throttle Slides §

![067_throttle_slides.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/067_throttle_slides.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle "Throttle Slide Circuit"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb4.htm

Throttle Slide

![068_throttle_slide_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_throttle_slide_2.jpg>)

![068_throttle_slide.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_throttle_slide.jpg>)

¶ Throttle Slides, sometimes called Throttle Valves, control the mixture from Idle to about 35% open. Yeah, I know, the Idle Circuit is supposed to control that. Well, it does and so does the Throttle Slide. Think of it as a relay race. As the racers on the different teams approach each other they sort of overlap so there is a smooth transition, of the baton, from one runner to the other. So it is with the Carburetor Circuits. We want a smooth transition from one Circuit of the Carburetor to another. Other then the cut out size, the slides can have a bevel cut out for left or right throttle stop adjustment

![068_right_throttle_stop_adjustment.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_right_throttle_stop_adjustment.jpg>)

. On some racing Carburetors there are no idle bevel cut out.

![068_some_racing_carburetors_there_no_idle_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_some_racing_carburetors_there_no_idle_2.jpg>)

![068_some_racing_carburetors_there_no_idle.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_some_racing_carburetors_there_no_idle.jpg>)

Throttle Slide Cutaway

![068_throttle_slide_cutaway_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_throttle_slide_cutaway_2.jpg>)

![068_throttle_slide_cutaway.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/068_throttle_slide_cutaway.jpg>)

Throttle Slide

The Throttle slide has a cut out on the inlet, Air Cleaner, side of the Carburetor Throat. This cut out makes the fuel mixture leaner or richer. Most people never change the Throttle Slide because the Slide is somewhat pricey, ranging from $50.00 to $80.00 and up. Also, I suspect most people don't even know that the Slide changes the fuel mixture. They think it just controls the throttle opening which, of course, it does in addition to controlling the just off Idle fuel mixture.

Come to think about it, in the last 50 years, I may have had about a million Carburetor Slides out of a million different Carburetors in my grimy little hands. I can't remember ever replacing one. Not even once. If you are smart enough to figure out that you need a 3.0 slide instead of the 2.5 slide you now have and you replace it AND the engine now runs better. Well, you are way above my pay grade. Why are you even reading this?

# Dan's Motorcycle "Needle Jet Circuit"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb5.htm

Needle Jet

![069_needle_jet_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_2.jpg>)

![069_needle_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet.jpg>)

The Needle Jet is located in the center of the Carburetor. The Jet Needle enters into the top of the Needle Jet and the Main Jet screws into the bottom. Poor, little Needle Jet. It sort of gets shafted and screwed at the same time. Needle Jets controls the fuel mixture from 15% to 60% open throttle. There seems to be three basic styles of Needle Jet.

Mikuni Primary style
Mikuni Bleed style
Keihin style

The Mikuni Primary style seems to be the most common. At least most all of the Carburetors I have worked on and have lying around are of this style. Next comes the Keihin style and then the Mikuni Bleed style. I am sure there are lots more styles out there but these seem to be the most common. Another thing they all have in common is that they all use an air bleed. Also, for the most part, they come in different sizes. At least the Mikunis do. I'm not totally sure about the Keihins. I haven't found any numbers on them.

![069_i_haven_t_found_any_numbers_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_i_haven_t_found_any_numbers_2.jpg>)

![069_i_haven_t_found_any_numbers.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_i_haven_t_found_any_numbers.jpg>)

Mikuni Primary Style

![069_mikuni_primary_style_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_mikuni_primary_style_2.jpg>)

![069_mikuni_primary_style.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_mikuni_primary_style.jpg>)

Keihin Style

![069_mikuni_primary_style_keihin_style_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_mikuni_primary_style_keihin_style_2.jpg>)

![069_mikuni_primary_style_keihin_style.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_mikuni_primary_style_keihin_style.jpg>)

Mikuni Bleed Style

If you look at the example below you will see the Primary style Needle Jet. that there is a round tube pressed into the top of the Needle Jet. Also notice there is a hole cut into one side of the Needle Jet. This hole is an air bleed from the Air Cleaner side of the Carburetor. It can just be a clear passage to the air in the Carburetor Bell or there can be an Air Jet screwed into that passage.

![069_can_just_clear_passage_air_carburetor_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_can_just_clear_passage_air_carburetor_2.jpg>)

![069_can_just_clear_passage_air_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_can_just_clear_passage_air_carburetor.jpg>)

Needle Jet sectioned

![069_needle_jet_sectioned_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_sectioned_2.jpg>)

![069_needle_jet_sectioned.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_sectioned.jpg>)

Needle Jet Center Tube

![069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center_3.jpg>)

![069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center.jpg>)

Needle Jet 1

![069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center_4.jpg>)

![069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_sectioned_needle_jet_center_2.jpg>)

needle Jet 2

The Needle jets are installed in the Carburetor in one of two ways. Both the Mikuni Primary and Bleed type Needle Jets are put in through the throat of the Carburetor and are held in the proper position by a pin and locked in position but the Main Jet and a washer

![069_washer.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_washer.jpg>)

of some kind. The Keihin type Needle Jet is held in by screwing the Needle Jet into the Carburetor. The Main Jet then screws into the bottom of the Needle Jet.

![069_main_jet_then_screws_into_bottom_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_main_jet_then_screws_into_bottom_2.jpg>)

![069_main_jet_then_screws_into_bottom.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_main_jet_then_screws_into_bottom.jpg>)

Needle Jet
Locating Pin

![069_needle_jet_locating_pin_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_locating_pin_2.jpg>)

![069_needle_jet_locating_pin.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_locating_pin.jpg>)

Mikuni Bleed style
Locating Pin Groove

![069_needle_jet_locating_pin_mikuni_bleed_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_locating_pin_mikuni_bleed_2.jpg>)

![069_needle_jet_locating_pin_mikuni_bleed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/069_needle_jet_locating_pin_mikuni_bleed.jpg>)

Keihin style
Screw-In Needle Jet

I'm sure there are other different Needle Jet styles but this probably covers 95 % of what is out there.

# Dan's Motorcycle "Jet Needle Circuit"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb6.htm

Jet Needle

![070_jet_needle_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_2.jpg>)

![070_jet_needle.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle.jpg>)

Jet Needles. Probably the most useful jet of all, at least to your average motorcycle tuner. The Jet Needle rides in the throttle slide. Jet Needles Come in lots of different sizes but the real beauty of the Jet Needle is it's adjustability. There is a clip and five little grooves that move the Jet Needle up (richer) or down (leaner) in the Needle Jet. Bad news is that many newer bikes have only one clip position. If you have a non-adjustable type, measure it and you may be able to get a replacement of the same size but with the five grooves. Another way is to place a small washer

![070_small_washer.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_small_washer.jpg>)

under the Jet Needle clip to richen the mixture. If you want to lean the mixture I guess you are out of luck. However, you probably will want to richen things up, so you should be OK.

The Jet Needle is held in the Throttle Side by a lot of different ways.

![070_different_ways.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_different_ways.jpg>)

Clips holding the Jet Needle to the slide seem to be popular. Also a little screw or even a plate held in by the throttle spring work good too.

![070_also_little_screw_even_plate_held_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_also_little_screw_even_plate_held_2.jpg>)

![070_also_little_screw_even_plate_held.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_also_little_screw_even_plate_held.jpg>)

Jet Needle clip

![070_jet_needle_clip_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_clip_2.jpg>)

![070_jet_needle_clip.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_clip.jpg>)

No Clip Needle Jets

![070_jet_needle_clip_no_clip_needle_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_clip_no_clip_needle_2.jpg>)

![070_jet_needle_clip_no_clip_needle.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_clip_no_clip_needle.jpg>)

Different Jet Needle Retainers

Jet Needles can be a simple taper or a be tapered in several stages.

![070_several_stages.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_several_stages.jpg>)

It controls the fuel mixture from about 20 % to 80 %. Jet Needles are easy to change, just move the clip. If you move the clip to a higher groove you lower the needle in the Needle Jet and make the mixture leaner. If you move the clip to a lower groove you raise the needle in the Needle Jet and make the mixture richer. Jet Needles cost around five dollars so you can afford to experiment with different sizes. All in all a very handy jet.

![070_all_all_very_handy_jet_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_all_all_very_handy_jet_2.jpg>)

![070_all_all_very_handy_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_all_all_very_handy_jet.jpg>)

Jet Needle in Needle Jet

![070_jet_needle_needle_jet_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_needle_jet_2.jpg>)

![070_jet_needle_needle_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/070_jet_needle_needle_jet.jpg>)

Throttle Slide and Jet Needle

# Dan's Motorcycle "Main Jet Circuit"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb7.htm

Main Jet

![071_main_jet_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/071_main_jet_2.jpg>)

![071_main_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/071_main_jet.jpg>)

¶
Main jets control the top two thirds to full throttle more or less. Main Jets are easy to change. They are probably the second most useful jet in the carburetor after the Jet Needle. Many Carburetors have a cap covering them so you can easily replace them without pulling the Carburetor off the engine. They can usually be removed with either a small screwdriver or a small wrench. Main Jets can be made of Brass or Plastic.

![071_main_jets_can_made_brass_plastic.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/071_main_jets_can_made_brass_plastic.jpg>)

Mikuni Main Jet Sizes

![071_section_main_jet_mikuni_main_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/071_section_main_jet_mikuni_main_jet.jpg>)

Mikuni Main Jet Cap

# Dan's Motorcycle "Carburetor Floats"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb8.htm

Carburetor Floats

![072_float.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_float.jpg>)

![072_carburetor_floats.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_carburetor_floats.jpg>)

¶

![072_cork.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_cork.jpg>)

![072_carburetor_floats_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_carburetor_floats_2.jpg>)

Carburetor Floats. They... well... Ah... float. Floats can be made out of metal or plastic or both.

![072_metal_plastic_both.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_metal_plastic_both.jpg>)

Back in the day they made them out of cork.

![072_carburetor_floats_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_carburetor_floats_2.jpg>)

Your Shop Manual will give you the correct height for each Carburetor. The Shop Manual will also tell you if you measure the Float height with or without the gasket. If you do not drain your Carburetors for winter you run the risk of water in your fuel freezing and crushing your Floats.

![072_crushing_floats.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_crushing_floats.jpg>)

Nothing like Gasohol to suck in that water. Think of it as the government's giving you one more reason to Winterize your engines.

Floats can be one piece or two piece. The theory being two piece Floats help keep a more accurate level when accelerating, decelerating and cornering.

![072_theory_being_two_piece_floats_help_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_theory_being_two_piece_floats_help_2.jpg>)

![072_theory_being_two_piece_floats_help.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_theory_being_two_piece_floats_help.jpg>)

One Piece Float

![072_one_piece_float_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_one_piece_float_2.jpg>)

![072_one_piece_float.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_one_piece_float.jpg>)

Two Piece Float

![072_one_piece_float_two_piece_float_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_one_piece_float_two_piece_float_2.jpg>)

![072_one_piece_float_two_piece_float.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_one_piece_float_two_piece_float.jpg>)

Find the float height specification in your shop manual. If it specifies measuring with the Float Bowel gasket, put it on. If not, leave it off. Turn the carb over and measure the distance from the Carburetor surface to the top of the float. I usually put a piece of tubing on the fuel inlet and very, very, gently blow in some air. With one finger very slowly raise the float. When you feel the air just start to release That is the float height. Measure that height and compare it to your Float height specification. Bend the Float Tang

![072_one_piece_float_two_piece_float.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_one_piece_float_two_piece_float.jpg>)

up or down to match that specification.

If you have double Floats you usually just make sure the Float lever is parallel with the Carburetor gasket surface. As always, check your Shop Manual.

![072_always_check_shop_manual_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_always_check_shop_manual_2.jpg>)

![072_always_check_shop_manual.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_always_check_shop_manual.jpg>)

Float Level Set Single Float

![072_float_level_set_single_float_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_float_level_set_single_float_2.jpg>)

![072_float_level_set_single_float.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/072_float_level_set_single_float.jpg>)

Float Level Set Double Float

# Dan's Motorcycle "Needle & Seat"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb8a.htm

Carburetor Fuel Valve
Needle and Seat

![073_needle_seat.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_needle_seat.jpg>)

![073_carburetor_fuel_valve_needle_seat.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_carburetor_fuel_valve_needle_seat.jpg>)

¶ Carburetor Fuel Valves, also known as Needle & Seat, fit to the Carburetor in one of three ways:

Screwed in
Pressed in
Held in with a clip and screw

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_2.jpg>)

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw.jpg>)

Screwed in Needle & Seat

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_6.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_6.jpg>)

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed.jpg>)

Pressed in Needle & Seat

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_7.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_7.jpg>)

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_2.jpg>)

Needle & Seat held in with a clip and screw

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_8.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_8.jpg>)

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_3.jpg>)

screwed in Needle & Seat

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_9.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_9.jpg>)

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_4.jpg>)

Pressed in Needle & Seat

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_10.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_10.jpg>)

![073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_5.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_screwed_pressed_held_clip_screw_screwed_5.jpg>)

Needle & Seat held in with a clip and screw

The Fuel inlet needles come in two forms:

Steel Tip
Rubber Tip

![073_steel_tip_rubber_tip.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_steel_tip_rubber_tip.jpg>)

Steel Tip Needle

![073_steel_tip_rubber_tip_steel_tip.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_steel_tip_rubber_tip_steel_tip.jpg>)

Rubber Tip Needle

Needle and Seats also come in different flow sizes. There are an astounding number of different Fuel Valve Needles. You would think four or five types would do it but no. Rubber Tip, Steel Tip and maybe a big one and a little one for more or less fuel flow but no. There must be a reason for so many seemingly similar Needles. However, if there is, I sure don't know what it would be. Maybe it is just to sell more parts, you think?

![073_maybe_just_sell_more_parts_think_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_maybe_just_sell_more_parts_think_2.jpg>)

![073_maybe_just_sell_more_parts_think.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_maybe_just_sell_more_parts_think.jpg>)

1.5 & 2.0 Needle Seats

![073_0_needle_seats_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_0_needle_seats_2.jpg>)

![073_0_needle_seats.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_0_needle_seats.jpg>)

Different Needles

![073_0_needle_seats_different_needles_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_0_needle_seats_different_needles_2.jpg>)

![073_0_needle_seats_different_needles.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_0_needle_seats_different_needles.jpg>)

Needle Clipped to Seat

I only know of one really innovative Fuel Valve. The Grose-Jet. I have only used it on one or two Carburetors and they worked just fine. You can still get them for some Carburetors but they are getting hard to find. The company who made them is still around but I don't know if they are still making them.

![073_company_who_made_them_still_around_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_company_who_made_them_still_around_2.jpg>)

![073_company_who_made_them_still_around.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_company_who_made_them_still_around.jpg>)

Grose-Jet 1

![073_grose_jet_1_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_grose_jet_1_2.jpg>)

![073_grose_jet_1.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_grose_jet_1.jpg>)

Grose-Jet 2

About the only thing you need to watch for on Jet Needles is wear on the end of the Needle. When you see the ring it is time to replace them. Another thing to remember is that very small bits of rust or dirt, from a dirty gas tank, can get caught on the seat of the Fuel Valve. This makes the Carburetor over flow. If this happens, take a plastic hammer or the plastic handle end of a screw driver and tap the Carburetor sharply. This will dislodge the obstruction and allow the Needle to seal against the seat. If, after tapping the Carburetor, it still leaks you need a new Needle & Seat.

![073_if_after_tapping_carburetor_still_leaks_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_if_after_tapping_carburetor_still_leaks_2.jpg>)

![073_if_after_tapping_carburetor_still_leaks.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_if_after_tapping_carburetor_still_leaks.jpg>)

Worn Fuel Valve Needles

![073_worn_fuel_valve_needles_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_worn_fuel_valve_needles_2.jpg>)

![073_worn_fuel_valve_needles.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_worn_fuel_valve_needles.jpg>)

Needle & Seat Sectioned

§ On to Air Jet Circuits §

![073_worn_fuel_valve_needles_needle_seat.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/073_worn_fuel_valve_needles_needle_seat.gif>)

![001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg>)

# Dan's Motorcycle "Air Jet"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb9.htm

Air Jet

![074_air_jet_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/074_air_jet_2.jpg>)

![074_air_jet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/074_air_jet.jpg>)

¶ Air Jets control the air that goes into the Needle Jet's air bleed. Air Jets come in three flavors.

Screw-in Air Jet.
Pressed-in Air Jet.
No Air Jet.

Air Jets control roughly the same range as the Main Jet. Sort of fine tunes the Main Jet. I doubt that you will be changing it much but you might.

# Dan's Motorcycle "Carburetor Tuning"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb10.htm

Carburetor Tuning

![075_tuning_jet_ranges.gif](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_tuning_jet_ranges.gif>)

![075_carburetor_tuning.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_carburetor_tuning.jpg>)

¶ OK, the drill is this. Make sure the engine is at normal operating temperature, not too hot or too cold. Now, with a new or very clean spark plug, run the engine, at the throttle position you want to test. Run the engine for a mile or two on a flat road. Now kill the ignition, chop the throttle (turn it off!), pull the clutch in and coast to a stop. Take the spark plug out and look at it. Does it read rich, normal or lean? Now comes the fun stuff. If you are not happy with the spark plug reading or how the engine performed you need to change a jet. You want smooth running in all throttle positions, with good plug color.

To help figure out which jet, throttle position is most important. Put a piece of masking tape around the throttle housing and a small piece on the throttle grip it's self. With the throttle shut, make coinciding marks on both pieces of tape. Now open the throttle wide open. Make another mark on the throttle housing matching the one you already made on the grip. Measure the distance between idle and full throttle. Divide that distance in quarters and put more marks on the tape. Now you can tell at what throttle settings the problem is occurring.

Now all this is real phony baloney as far as preciseness is concerned. Don't waste your time getting minute of arc accuracy although I suppose it would not hurt. Remember everything overlaps. You just want to know the general area or throttle position where the problem lies. Then adjust the jet(s) that control that area. Then Retest.

This can be a great (?) way to spend your yearly two week vacation. I once watched a friend do exactly that. He put a gigantic Mikuni Carburetor on a 350cc Honda single. It came pre-set supposedly. That was a joke. It ran as smooth as stock when he finished. No extra power but it was one BIG Carburetor. I told him it would not get him any extra power but no one ever listens to me. I'm used to it.

Yeah, I know, this might take forever... or not! Who knows. Some people get it on the very first try but not me. The factories have Dynamometers and other fancy stuff. This makes everything a lot easier, not to mention safer. Roaring down the road at 120 MPH trying to get a Main Jet reading is not as fun as it might first appear.

![075_roaring_down_road_120_mph_trying_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_roaring_down_road_120_mph_trying_2.jpg>)

![075_roaring_down_road_120_mph_trying.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_roaring_down_road_120_mph_trying.jpg>)

Throttle Marks 1

![075_throttle_marks_1_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_throttle_marks_1_2.jpg>)

![075_throttle_marks_1.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_throttle_marks_1.jpg>)

Throttle Marks 2

Another thing to consider is the fact that engines change over time as their parts wear and engine compression changes. As the engine compression goes down, over time and miles, the suction or vacuum in the Carburetor Venturi is less then it was when the engine was new. Because there is less suction there tends to be less fuel mixture pulled into the engine so the engine may run a bit lean. The cure is bigger (Richer) jets. This can happen in reverse when you put on a big bore kit. The bigger engine can suck too much fuel mixture making the engine run rich. Smaller (Leaner) jets cure this.

Make sure the engine is a normal operating temperature. If the engine is too hot or too cold it will run funny. If you just need a touch more richness try running the fuel level at the highest level. Usually the float level specifications have a plus/minus range. If the level is just a bit higher it is easier for the engine vacuum to suck in the fuel. Same with if it is a bit lower, it will be harder to suck in the fuel. This effect is very, very, minimal but might be useful to you.

Basically, if the engine is not running right, it is running either too rich or too lean. Here are some vague, but perhaps useful things to look for.
Fuel mixture is too rich.

Engine noise is dull and intermittent
Things get worse when choke or enrichener is turned on.
Things get worse when engine gets hot.
If you remove the air cleaner, things get somewhat better.
Exhaust fumes are heavy.
Spark plug is fouled black, dry and sooty.

Fuel mixture is too lean.

Engine gets over heated.
Things improves when choke or enrichener is turned on.
Acceleration is poor.
Spark plug is whitish or burned.
Engine Speed fluctuates. Noticeable Lack of power.

![075_noticeable_lack_power_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_noticeable_lack_power_2.jpg>)

![075_noticeable_lack_power.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_noticeable_lack_power.jpg>)

Jet Ranges 1

![075_jet_ranges_1_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_2.jpg>)

![075_jet_ranges_1.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1.jpg>)

Jet Ranges 2

![075_carburetor_jets.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_carburetor_jets.jpg>)

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2.jpg>)

Carburetor Parts

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_6.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_6.jpg>)

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_2.jpg>)

Idle Cutaway

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_7.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_7.jpg>)

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_3.jpg>)

Quarter Throttle Cutaway

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_8.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_8.jpg>)

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_4.jpg>)

Three Quarters Throttle Cutaway

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_9.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_9.jpg>)

![075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_5.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/075_jet_ranges_1_jet_ranges_2_5.jpg>)

Full Throttle Cutaway

So this is the end of my Bloviation on Carburetors for now. Hopfully my idle words have helped you to understand the inner workings of your Mechanical Slide Carburetor a little better.

# Dan's Motorcycle "Start Mixture Enrichment Circuit"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb11.htm

Start Mixture Enrichment Circuit

![076_start_mixture_enrichment_circuit_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_start_mixture_enrichment_circuit_2.jpg>)

![076_start_mixture_enrichment_circuit.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_start_mixture_enrichment_circuit.jpg>)

¶ A cold engine does not vaporize fuel well. Gasoline will ony burn when it is vaporized. Therefore, you have to put in a larger amount of raw gas then normal, so enough of it will vaporize. Then it will be able to burn and start the engine.

Mikuni Carburetors do this with a Mixture Enrichement Circuit. This circuit takes fuel from the float bowl, air from the front of the Carburetor and funnels it into the front of the Carburetor. For this Mixture Enrichment Circuit to work the Throttle Slide MUST be closed. This allows for a high vacuum to be present. If you open the throttle it lessens the vacuum considerably. This stops the Mixture Enrichement Circuit from working. The Mixture Enrichement Circuit is activated by a plunger.

![076_plunger.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger.jpg>)

Most Mixture Enrichement Circuits plungers are activated in one of three ways.

Plunger Knob
Plunger Lever
Plunger Cable

![076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_4.jpg>)

![076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable.jpg>)

Plunger Knob Type

![076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_5.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_5.jpg>)

![076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_2.jpg>)

Plunger Lever Type

![076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_6.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_6.jpg>)

![076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_plunger_knob_plunger_lever_plunger_cable_3.jpg>)

Plunger Cable Type

The plunger is raised. Vacuum from the front of the Carburetor pulls air, from the rear of the Carburetor. It mixes that air with fuel coming through a small, pressed in, jet in the bottom of the Carburetor Float Bowl. The fuel goes from that jet through a passage in the Float Bowl. Flows up a tube and out the Plunger orifice. Then the fuel/air mixture goes through a passage to the front of the Carburetor and into the engine.

![076_then_fuel_air_mixture_goes_through_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_then_fuel_air_mixture_goes_through_2.jpg>)

![076_then_fuel_air_mixture_goes_through.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_then_fuel_air_mixture_goes_through.jpg>)

Starter Jet Intake

![076_starter_jet_intake_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_2.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake.jpg>)

Starter Jet Outlet

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_7.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_7.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet.jpg>)

Starter Jet Fuel Pipe

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_8.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_8.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_2.jpg>)

Starter Jet Fuel Passage

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_9.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_9.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_3.jpg>)

Brass Starter Jet

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_10.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_10.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_4.jpg>)

Starter Plunger orifice

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_11.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_11.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_5.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_5.jpg>)

Starter Plunger

Starter Plungers can be found on multi-cylinder engines too.

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_12.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_12.jpg>)

![076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_6.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_starter_jet_intake_starter_jet_outlet_6.jpg>)

Other Carburetor Manufacturers use a different way of getting there. If you look closely you will see the Bing uses a cable operated, round piece of metal to do the same thing the plunger does. Cover and uncover the Starter Jet Port. One way or another they all end up at the same place. We have to have more gas going in to get a cold engine started.

![076_we_have_have_more_gas_going_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_we_have_have_more_gas_going_2.jpg>)

![076_we_have_have_more_gas_going.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_we_have_have_more_gas_going.jpg>)

![076_bing_auxiliary_starter_carburetor_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_bing_auxiliary_starter_carburetor_2.jpg>)

![076_bing_auxiliary_starter_carburetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/076_bing_auxiliary_starter_carburetor.jpg>)

Bing Auxiliary Starter Carburetor

Some Scooters have special electric Starter Plungers. Most are on Scooters. In the last 30 years I have had about, oh, maybe four or five scooters come in the shop. I am in the State of Idaho, USA. In some big cities or overseas they seem to be quite popular but not here. To learn more about them check your Scooter's shop manual.

# Dan's Motorcycle "Choke Plates"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/carb12.htm

Carburetor Choke Plates

![077_starter_circuit.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_starter_circuit.jpg>)

![077_carburetor_choke_plates.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_carburetor_choke_plates.jpg>)

¶ When you choke something it means you restrict the air coming in. On a Carburetor we do this with a plate of some kind that drops down and restricts the air coming into the engine. The thing is this. As the Electric Starter or Kick Starter cranks the engine, the engine is sucking away (Vacuum) and instead of sucking air, which is restricted (Choked) it starts sucking extra fuel from the Needle Jet and the Idle Jet Port. That extra fuel enables the engine to start. I have only seen Choke Plates come in two styles.

Guillotine Style
Plate Style

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_2.jpg>)

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style.jpg>)

Guillotine Style Choke

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_4.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_4.jpg>)

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style.jpg>)

Guillotine Style Choke top

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_5.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_5.jpg>)

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_2.jpg>)

Choke Plate Style On

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_6.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_6.jpg>)

![077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_3.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_guillotine_style_plate_style_guillotine_style_3.jpg>)

Choke Plate Style Off

Some Plate Chokes are spring loaded. The spring keeps them closed. The lever pushes them open. One thing to remember on Spring Loaded Plate Chokes. If the spring breaks, the Choke does not work right. Trouble is, it is not always obvious the spring is broken. So the Choke is not working and you crank and crank, overheat the very expensive starter and burn it out. If you think the Choke is on but the engine will not start, feel the Choke Lever with your hand and make sure the spring is not broken.

![077_if_think_choke_but_engine_will_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_if_think_choke_but_engine_will_2.jpg>)

![077_if_think_choke_but_engine_will.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_if_think_choke_but_engine_will.jpg>)

Choke Plate

![077_choke_plate_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_choke_plate_2.jpg>)

![077_choke_plate.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_choke_plate.jpg>)

Choke Plate Levers

Some Choke Plates, not all, have little, spring loaded doors in the plate. This is because some engines need a bit more air if the vacuum gets too high in the Carburetor throat.

![077_because_some_engines_need_bit_more_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_because_some_engines_need_bit_more_2.jpg>)

![077_because_some_engines_need_bit_more.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_because_some_engines_need_bit_more.jpg>)

Spring Loaded door in Choke Plate

![077_spring_loaded_door_choke_plate_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_spring_loaded_door_choke_plate_2.jpg>)

![077_spring_loaded_door_choke_plate.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_spring_loaded_door_choke_plate.jpg>)

Spring Loaded door in Choke Plate

Back in the day there were some Amal Carburetors that had the choke (Air Valve) inside the Throttle Slide. You will probably never run across one of these Chokes. Curiously enough you can still buy a brand new Monobloc Carburetor from Amal. About £ 134.00 British Pounds or about $200.00 USA dollars. As of March, 2015.

![077_march_2015_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_march_2015_2.jpg>)

![077_march_2015.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_march_2015.jpg>)

Amal Monobloc Carbutetor

![077_amal_monobloc_carbutetor_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_amal_monobloc_carbutetor_2.jpg>)

![077_amal_monobloc_carbutetor.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_amal_monobloc_carbutetor.jpg>)

Amal Monobloc
Choke/Air Valve
In Throttle Slide

![077_amal_monobloc_carbutetor_amal_monobloc_choke_2.jpg](<04_Fuel_Carburetors/077_amal_monobloc_carbutetor_amal_monobloc_choke_2.jpg>)
