# Dan's Motorcycle "Honing Your Cylinder"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/hone_cyl.htm

Hone Your Cylinder

![113_hone_cylinder_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_hone_cylinder_2.jpg>)

![113_hone_cylinder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_hone_cylinder.jpg>)

¶ Honing a cylinder can go from mild to wild. If the cylinder is within specification and you are only going to put in a new set of rings, you must hone the cylinder to break the glaze. This will put a nice crosshatch pattern in the cylinder walls. The crosshatch pattern will hold oil and help lubricate the piston and rings as the rings wear in to the cylinder. That is mild. A cylinder hone can also be used to bore a cylinder to a bigger size and that is wild. Well... yeah, your right. I need to get a life if I think that is wild!

Cylinder hones can also be used to hone brake cylinders, clutch cylinders and most any round cylinder. Cylinder hones can be fairly cheap in price, around five dollars, or quite expensive. Ammco and Sunnen hones can cost hundreds of dollars. The cheap ones work well for cleaning up a spot of rust or breaking the glaze. The expensive ones can accurately bore a cylinder to accept the next oversize piston or bigger.

![113_hone_cylinder_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_hone_cylinder_3.jpg>)

![113_expensive_ones_can_accurately_bore_cylinder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_expensive_ones_can_accurately_bore_cylinder.jpg>)

To Hone a cylinder is easy.

![113_expensive_ones_can_accurately_bore_cylinder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_expensive_ones_can_accurately_bore_cylinder.jpg>)

Just stick the hone in the cylinder, slobber on some oil and have at it. Move the hone back and forth in the cylinder to produce a 45 degree cross hatch pattern

![113_move_hone_back_forth_cylinder_produce.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_move_hone_back_forth_cylinder_produce.jpg>)

and in a minute or so your done. That is assuming you don't need to bore it oversize. If the cylinder is well worn you will have to bore it oversize. In a cylinder that is grossly worn out, the piston, set at top-dead-center, will wiggle forward and back in the bore. This tells us two things. One, you need to bore the cylinder oversize and two, you are sadly lacking in your maintenance. If the piston is fairly tight you might be able to get away with just a hone job and a set of new rings. If you are unsure you will need to measure the piston clearance. You will need inside

![017_inside.jpg](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/017_inside.jpg>)

and outside

![017_outside.jpg](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/017_outside.jpg>)

micrometers to accurately make the measurements.

The procedure is simple but you must be very precise in it's execution.

Measure the diameter of the piston about one half inch up the skirt.
Measure the diameter of the cylinder at:

Both front to back and side to side.
Measured at top, middle and bottom of the cylinder.

![113_measured_top_middle_bottom_cylinder_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measured_top_middle_bottom_cylinder_2.jpg>)

![113_measured_top_middle_bottom_cylinder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measured_top_middle_bottom_cylinder.jpg>)

Measure Piston

![113_measure_piston_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston_2.jpg>)

![113_measure_piston.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston.jpg>)

Measure Cylinder

![113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder_2.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder_2.gif>)

![113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder.gif>)

Measure Cylinder Places
Four Stroke

![113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder_measure_cylinder_2.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder_measure_cylinder_2.gif>)

![113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder_measure_cylinder.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston_measure_cylinder_measure_cylinder.gif>)

Measure Cylinder Places
Two Stroke.

Take the piston measurement

![113_measured_top_middle_bottom_cylinder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measured_top_middle_bottom_cylinder.jpg>)

and subtract it from the biggest cylinder measurement.

![113_measure_piston.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_measure_piston.jpg>)

Compare the result with the piston clearance given by the manufacturer of the piston. In other words if the cylinder measures 2.6114" and you subtract the pistons diameter of 2.609" you get .0024". Compare that to the piston manufacturers suggested minimum/maximum clearance. In this case that would be .0016"-.003" with a limit of .004". If it is within that specification you could hone the cylinder and put in a new set of rings. If it is OVER that specification you will need to bore the cylinder out to the next biggest oversize and buy a new piston and rings.

![113_hone_marks.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_hone_marks.jpg>)

![113_if_over_specification_will_need_bore.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_if_over_specification_will_need_bore.jpg>)

The reason you take so many measurements is because cylinders can wear at different rates at different spots in the cylinder. The most wear occurs at the top of the cylinder and in the front and back portion of the cylinder. The least wear is at the bottom of the cylinder. Sometimes, you can even see slight hone marks

![113_if_over_specification_will_need_bore.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_if_over_specification_will_need_bore.jpg>)

at the bottom of the cylinder, even after many miles. The cylinder wears in a taper and out of round from the top down.

Sometimes the wear is so pronounced that there is a ring worn

![113_ring_worn.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_ring_worn.jpg>)

into the cylinder

![113_cylinder_ridge.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_cylinder_ridge.jpg>)

![113_ring_worn.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_ring_worn.jpg>)

just below the top of the cylinder at the spot where the rings stop. On engines that have their pistons installed from the bottom of the cylinder the ridge does not matter much for disassembly. On engines that have to have their pistons installed from the top of the cylinder there is a problem. The rings tend to catch on that ridge so you have to use a special tool called a Ridge Reamer

![113_ridge_reamer.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_ridge_reamer.jpg>)

to cut the ridge out the ridge.

Cheap Hones

![113_hone_cylinder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_hone_cylinder.jpg>)

will brake the glaze but not much more. At least if you try to do more you are in for a real fun time. The problem is that you can't hold the taper and out of roundness with any kind of accuracy. This is not to say this can't be done, just that it is very hard to do. I once read of a man in India. He saw a young boy of about twelve years old slowly bore out a cylinder with a rat tail file. He said every day when he walked by this little mechanic shop he saw the boy working on the cylinder with that file. It took about five full days of work before he did it. That kid was a better mechanic then I'll ever be! At least he had more patience then I have. I totally believe the story. It could be done... just not in the USA.

![113_sunnen_hone.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_sunnen_hone.jpg>)

![113_just_not_usa.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_just_not_usa.jpg>)

![113_ammco_hone.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_ammco_hone.jpg>)

![113_just_not_usa_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_just_not_usa_2.jpg>)

This is not to say I haven't bored out some wild and crazy holes. In my wayward youth, for a friend, I once bored out a Briggs and Stratton cylinder, to the next oversize, with a ball hone.

![113_ball_hone.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_ball_hone.jpg>)

It actually worked too! Unfortunately, a motorcycle cylinder requires a bit more precision. Boring with a hone takes a long time. Like several hours. I once honed a cylinder .040" oversize. I held it to the right taper and out of roundness but it took a long, long time. You need a quality hone, I used an Ammco hone. Then you hone a bit and then you measure. Hone a bit and then measure. It takes hours and is very, well, boring! When you are finished you want a nice 45 degree angle cross hatch pattern

![113_move_hone_back_forth_cylinder_produce.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_move_hone_back_forth_cylinder_produce.jpg>)

in the bore. Never hone a cylinder dry. Use lots of oil when honing. Buy the special honing oil. It works much better then plain oil. Honing oil cools the cylinder and hone. It also enhances the cutting effect of the stones. Use a lot of honing oil!

The best way to bore a cylinder is to use a boring machine and not a hone. If you do use a hone you must use a high quality one like a Sunnen or an Ammco hone. Hones come in several sizes to fit different cylinder bores. Some of the Ammco hones have several sizes

![113_several_sizes.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/113_several_sizes.jpg>)

of stones so you can use a standard size hone in a large cylinder bore. The Ammco hones also come in several grit sizes. Coarse (60), fine (220) and super fine (320) for aluminum and plated cylinders. Some top-of-the-line hones use diamond impregnated stones but those are priced a bit out of my price range.

I suppose you could try to bore a cylinder with just about any hone but you need to remember this. You MUST hold out of roundness to .001-.002" inch OR less. Taper MUST be less then .001-.002" top to bottom. Shoot for .001" on both! The real trouble comes when the cylinder is already worn oval and tapered. A regular cheap hone will just keep wearing more taper and out of roundness. A good hone is rigidly made and if you are careful, it will pull the cylinder back into round. Start in the lower portion of the cylinder where there is almost no wear and the bore is perfectly round. From there you can work your way on up the cylinder. It is not so hard. It's just time consuming. Like the young boy in India. You have to be patient. You just have to hone a bit and measure, then hone a bit and measure. Continue till you get to the size you desire. The big problem is the time it takes. Removing .010" is not so bad but .020" or .040" takes a long time.

Resist the urge to put the hone in a drill press, kick her on high and have at it. Been there, done that. Didn't work so good. Slow, steady, and lots and lots of measurements. That is the way to go.

A better way to go is to use a boring machine. The bore job will be more accurate.

If the cylinder you are boring is from a two stroke, chamfer or break the edge of the ports with a file so the rings do not get caught on edges. A ball hone works great for this. Also remember to check the power valve. If it extends into the cylinder after boring it will have to be ground down so no part of it can touch the piston.

You can hone plated cylinders but only just a bit. All you want is to make a cross hatch pattern to help the rings seat. You may need to buy special stones depending on the kind of plating of the cylinder. Check with the manufacturer to be sure.

When you are finished, clean the cylinder with clean solvent and then wash it in warm soapy water. Then take a clean rag and put some fresh oil on it. Now wipe the newly honed cylinder down with it. If you see any dirt on the rag rewash the cylinder and wipe it down again. Do this until the rag comes up clean.

When all is said and done the best way is this. Measure the cylinder and piston. If the clearance is within specification, hone the cylinder a bit, put in new rings and drive on. If you must bore for an oversize piston, get the piston, get the correct clearance, take both and the cylinder to a machine shop that bores cylinders and let them bore it. This is the best and cheapest way to get the job done right.

![113_best_cheapest_way_get_job_done.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/113_best_cheapest_way_get_job_done.gif>)

![113_best_cheapest_way_get_job_done.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/113_best_cheapest_way_get_job_done.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle "Chinese Motorcycle Rings"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/rings.htm

Chinese Motorcycle Rings

![114_chinese_motorcycle_rings.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_chinese_motorcycle_rings.jpg>)

¶ Rings have a mark on the side of the ring that goes up. This mark can be either a printed (Like with ink) mark or a mark stamped into the ring. Unfortunately, a lot of Chinese rings... well... don't! People keep asking me "If there is no mark, which way do the rings go?" I never really gave it much thought till I started working on some Chinese engines. Now, all of a sudden, this is an issue. After looking at a lot of ring sets and studying a lot of shop manuals, here is my best guess.

![114_chrome_plated_top_ring.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_chrome_plated_top_ring.jpg>)

![114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying.jpg>)

![114_second_tapered_ring.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_second_tapered_ring.jpg>)

![114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying_2.jpg>)

On four stroke engines the top ring is often chrome plated

![114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying.jpg>)

on the sliding surface. If it has a taper

![114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_after_looking_lot_ring_sets_studying_2.jpg>)

on the back side of the ring that taper should go up and it should be the second ring. If the front side of the ring is tapered, the taper should be up. I realize that some ring designs have a stepped or taper side that is meant to be installed down but I have not come across any being used in a motorcycle engine. Just because I have not run across them does not mean that they are not out there.

![114_parkerized_ring.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_parkerized_ring.jpg>)

![114_just_because_i_have_not_run.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_just_because_i_have_not_run.jpg>)

If the ring is not chromed it probably would be the second ring and again the tapered edge in the back of the ring should go up. Same on the front side. If there is a taper it should go up. These black rings have a parkerized coating

![114_just_because_i_have_not_run.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_just_because_i_have_not_run.jpg>)

that increases their resistance to wear. Sometimes the parkerized ring is used as the first or top ring too.

The three piece oil rings

![114_three_piece_oil_rings.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_rings.jpg>)

have no up or down side.

![114_three_piece_oil_ring.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_ring.jpg>)

![114_three_piece_oil_rings.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_rings.jpg>)

![114_bevel_end.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_bevel_end.jpg>)

![114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no.jpg>)

![114_ring_expander.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_ring_expander.jpg>)

![114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no_2.jpg>)

Some two strokes have a bevel at the ends of the ring

![114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no.jpg>)

, or the beginning, depending on your point of view. That bevel fits the peg in the piston. This bevel goes up. If there are two rings and one is chrome plated, the plated one goes in the top ring groove. If both rings are plated and one has a taper the tapered one is the second ring. Sometimes the second ring will have a ring expander

![114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_three_piece_oil_rings_have_no_2.jpg>)

behind it. Also check the thickness of the ring because sometimes the top and second ring can be of different thicknesses. I have not seen any Keystone

![114_keystone.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_keystone.jpg>)

or Dykes

![114_dykes.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/114_dykes.jpg>)

type rings from China but you never know what the future will bring! Make sure the ring compresses completely and smoothly into the ring groove. If it does not, it is not the right ring for the groove. As far as I know Keystone and Dykes rings are ONLY used on two stroke engines. At least, I have never seen them used on four stroke engines.

To identify a Keystone ring place one side of the ring in the jaws of a vernier caliper and clamp down on it firmly. Now move the opposite side of the ring up and down. If it is a flat ring it will not rock. It will only flex. If it IS a Keystone type ring it wll rock until the Keystone edge hits the jaw of the caliper.

I have noticed that most Chinese engines, at this time (2010), don't have oversize pistons available. If an engine has run enough to require new rings and/or piston, the cylinder is almost always worn out too and requires either boring to the next oversize or replacement.

If it sounds like the Chinese need to MARK THEIR RINGS AND HAVE OVERSIZES, You would be right.

![114_if_sounds_like_chinese_need_mark.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/114_if_sounds_like_chinese_need_mark.gif>)

![114_if_sounds_like_chinese_need_mark.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/114_if_sounds_like_chinese_need_mark.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle " Gear Boxes "

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/gearbox.htm

![115_gearboxes_motorcycle_engines_do_not_produce.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_gearboxes_motorcycle_engines_do_not_produce.jpg>)

GEARBOXES

¶ Motorcycle engines do not produce all their power at all RPM's. There is very little power at idle
and the power goes up as the engine RPM goes up. At a certain RPM, which is different for each engine, the power goes up quickly
and continues to increase until it hits the maximum RPM for that engine. This is called the "Power Band". Generally
small, high revving 2/strokes have a narrow power band, requiring lots of gears in the gear box. Large, low revving 4/strokes, have a big
power band and don't need so many gears.

Anyway you go, you need some kind of Gearbox to keep the engine RPM within it's power band, while providing the bike with a
good acceleration, and speed range. While there are lots of styles and types of gear boxes, I think they all seem to boil down to
three different crankcase types.

Horizontally split...

![115_horizontally_split_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_horizontally_split_2.jpg>)

![115_horizontally_split.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_horizontally_split.jpg>)

... The crankcase has a seam on the horizontal plane. All multi cylinder I have seen are split Horizontally. This means you do not have to take the Cylinder Head off to replace a gear.

Vertically split...

![115_vertically_split_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_vertically_split_2.jpg>)

![115_vertically_split.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_vertically_split.jpg>)

... The crankcase has a seam on the vertical plane. Most single cylinder engines are split vertically but not all of them. The Honda XR/XL175

![115_xr_xl175.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_xr_xl175.jpg>)

comes to mind.

Cassette type...

![115_cassette_type_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_cassette_type_2.jpg>)

![115_cassette_type.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_cassette_type.jpg>)

... The gears are loaded in from one side. Like a Cassette tape. Triumph, BSA, and Harley-Davidson Sportsters have used this style of Gearbox.

Back in the day, say before mid 1950s, the Gearboxes were separate from the engines on a lot of machines but now-a-days the engines and Gearboxes are all one unit.

Most all of the Gearboxes on motorcycles are "constant mesh". That means all the gears are constantly meshed with one another and are always spinning.
Because of this, there are no synchros to speed up the gears when they engage, like there are in automotive Gearboxes.

![115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_3.jpg>)

![115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up.jpg>)

![115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_4.jpg>)

![115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_2.jpg>)

In the motorcycle gearbox there are two shafts. In most of them,

![115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up.jpg>)

the one with the clutch on the end of it is the main shaft. The other is the countershaft and it has the
countershaft sprocket on one end of it. A few

![115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_because_there_no_synchros_speed_up_2.jpg>)

have the clutch and counter sprocket on the same shaft. Some of the gears are fixed and/or machined to the transmission shafts. The other gears slide or spin on these shafts.
The gears that slide back and forth on the shafts have what are called Dogs.

![115_dogs.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_dogs.jpg>)

These Dogs are knobs of metal that fit into holes in the gears beside them,
locking the two gears together.

The sliding gears are moved back and forth by Shifter Forks which in turn are moved by a shifter drum.
The Shifter Forks are usually attached to the Shifter Drum

![115_shifter_drum.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_drum.jpg>)

or move in a groove

![115_groove.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_groove.jpg>)

machined in the Shifter Drum.
This drum is turned or rotated, through different styles of linkages, by the gear Shifter Shaft Linkage.

![115_shifter_shaft_linkage.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_shaft_linkage.jpg>)

![115_drum_turned_rotated_through_different_styles.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_drum_turned_rotated_through_different_styles.jpg>)

![115_shifter_drum.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_drum.jpg>)

Shifter Drum

![115_shifter_drum_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_drum_2.jpg>)

![115_groove.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_groove.jpg>)

Shifter Drum with Grooves

![115_shifter_drum_shifter_drum_grooves.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_drum_shifter_drum_grooves.jpg>)

![115_shifter_shaft_linkage.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_shaft_linkage.jpg>)

Shifter Shaft Linkage

As the gears move back and forth
they lock the main shaft and counter shaft together thru each set of gears, giving us 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc.

![115_1st_2nd_3rd_etc.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_1st_2nd_3rd_etc.jpg>)

A few use a grooved plate to move the shift forks.

While the design of the Gearbox is complicated, fixing, repairing, or overhauling it really isn't. However, there are a few things to watch for.

![115_power_path.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_power_path.jpg>)

![115_1st_2nd_3rd_etc.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_1st_2nd_3rd_etc.jpg>)

Always put everything back in EXACTLY the same position as when you removed it. Many shafts or gears can go in backwards and work just fine, BUT
you will have reversed the wear pattern, and the parts will have to re-wear themselves into each other. This increases the wear on your
parts for no good reason. So if for nothing more than the general principal of the thing, always reinstall parts in the exact position they were in. If necessary
mark them with a Marks-a-lot felt tip pen.

When you pull the gears out, DON'T just dump the gears out on the floor like a sack of potatoes.
Pull them out gently, as a unit. On some it is best to pull both shafts, drum and the shift forks together. On others it's best to
remove the shafts that hold the shifter forks and remove them first, then the drum, and then the gear clusters. On some makes the
gears are kept on the shafts by circlips. On others, the gears can fall right off. Often there are shims

![115_shims.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shims.jpg>)

( thin, large washers ) on the ends
of the shafts. These shims are used to position the gears and take up any side play, so look for them when you pull any shaft out. They tend to stick to the bearings.
You may need to clean the part of the counter shaft that is outside the crankcase. You know, where the countershaft sprocket is. Get all that rust and dirt off it, so it will slide on out through the bearing.

![115_egg_crate.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_egg_crate.jpg>)

![115_get_all_rust_dirt_off_so.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_get_all_rust_dirt_off_so.jpg>)

When you disassemble the gear shafts, use a cardboard egg crate

![115_get_all_rust_dirt_off_so.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_get_all_rust_dirt_off_so.jpg>)

to hold the gear parts in the order that you disassemble them.

![115_worn_shift_fork.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_worn_shift_fork.jpg>)

![115_when_disassemble_gear_shafts_use_cardboard.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_when_disassemble_gear_shafts_use_cardboard.jpg>)

If the transmission wants to jump out of gear, usually second gear, under power, take a good look at both the Dogs and the holes they fit in and the sides
of the Shifter Forks

![115_when_disassemble_gear_shafts_use_cardboard.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_when_disassemble_gear_shafts_use_cardboard.jpg>)

for wear. If there is any wear at all on these parts replace them.

If the gear has broken teeth

![115_broken_teeth.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_broken_teeth.jpg>)

it is a good idea to replace both it and its mate on the other gear shaft.
Normally broken teeth make quite a bit of noise. Sometimes, there is a lot of noise, but when you get the gear out... nothing looks broken. Look for
a bent tooth, or a tooth with a bit of debris stuck on it. It could be a bit of steel, aluminum, who knows what, it can still make noise.

![115_gear_teeth.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_gear_teeth.jpg>)

![115_could_bit_steel_aluminum_who_knows.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_could_bit_steel_aluminum_who_knows.jpg>)

When you inspect the gear teeth, you will notice that, on almost all them, there are a lot more pits and wear lines than what we would like to see. These gears are from a well worn Honda CR480. A powerful bike back in the day. On this example the crankcase around the main crank bearing broke. The gears, pits and all, were going strong.

All the books say replace them... but man... if I did that, I'd have to replace them all. That would cost a lot of cash. So it's a judgment call you will have to make. If they are really
bad, replace them. Just be sure to take into account the cost of the gears verses the worth of the machine and its power output. Expensive, high power
machines deserve and require good gears, but a $500 machine does not need $500 worth of new gears.

Gearbox Bearings are another judgment call. They run in an oil bath and rarely wear out. Even if the oil level is run low the gear
box bearings probably get more oil than the average 2/stroke main bearing. As with gears if they look OK they Probably are. If it's
a high power, expensive, machine...put in new. Cheapo machine? Just live with them.

Now, speaking of living with it...sometimes a Gearbox will loose a gear... bang, it's gone. Now, you can run through all the gears, everything sounds OK, but
one of the gears is just not there anymore. Can you ignore it and just drive on? I think you can. Yes, there is always the risk that whatever broke could get jammed
in other parts of the Gearbox, locking everything up and doing a lot of damage. Do you want to risk it? I think the odds are good that you will not have any
problems, except your missing a gear. But understand, there is a RISK.
OK, now you assemble the gear clusters and put them and everything else back in the crankcases, with lots of oil, of course. Now you try to shift through all the gears,
and man, it shifts sort of hard. Did you do something wrong? Maybe not. If you were careful on assembly and the gear shafts turn easily, just make sure you can shift thru
all the gears. It helps to spin the gear shafts by hand as you shift to help things slide into position. If it's just a bit hard, kind of chunky, so to speak, you are OK. When it's spinning
fast, it will work just fine.

AUTOMATIC TRANSMISSIONS

Yes, there are motorcycles with Automatic Transmissions. Honda had a 750cc and a 400cc, Suzuki had a 450cc, and Moto Guzzi had a 1000cc automatic. These were true automatics.

Most were made in the late 70's, early 80's and had a 2-speed gear box with a torque converter

![115_torque_converter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_torque_converter.jpg>)

. I've ridden the Honda 750 and it was...well... automatic. With two speeds it was
no ball-of-fire, but it was OK. You don't see them around much and as I have never worked on one, I probably shouldn't try to tell you how to fix one.
Rokon

![115_rokon.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_rokon.jpg>)

Had a 340cc dirt bike with a snowmobile type, belt drive, transmission with drive and driven clutches. Rokon also
has a two wheel drive, backwoods, motorcycle with the same type of clutch. Works quilt well once you get used to it. It will go just about anywhere.

![001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg>)

![115_will_go_just_about_anywhere.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/115_will_go_just_about_anywhere.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle " Gear Boxes "

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/cassette_tape.htm

Cassettes

¶ It has been pointed out to me that some of you younger folks, and to me anyone under sixty is a younger folk, may not know what a Cassette is. A Cassette is a unit of something - gears, tape, whatever - that slides inside some kind of holder or player.

![115_cassette_unit_something_gears_tape_whatever_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_cassette_unit_something_gears_tape_whatever_2.jpg>)

![115_cassette_unit_something_gears_tape_whatever.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_cassette_unit_something_gears_tape_whatever.jpg>)

BSA Cassette Gearbox

![115_bsa_cassette_gearbox_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_bsa_cassette_gearbox_2.jpg>)

![115_bsa_cassette_gearbox.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_bsa_cassette_gearbox.jpg>)

Mini Cassette

Back in the Days of Yore we had big, black, twelve inch diameter, CDs. We called them Records. Now-a-day those are just called Vinyl. Vinyl Records were what the real modern, hip people used instead of Reel to Reel tape. But Records were big and had to be played on big Record Players

![115_record_players.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_record_players.jpg>)

. We wanted to be cool and carry our vibes with us. Trouble was, our vibes had to go on Records or tape. They came out with small, portable, Reel to Reel recorders but you still had to thread and wind the tape on each tape. Not cool.

![115_not_cool.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_not_cool.jpg>)

![115_not_cool.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_not_cool.jpg>)

Reel to Reel

![115_reel_reel_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_reel_reel_2.jpg>)

![115_reel_reel.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_reel_reel.jpg>)

Vinyl Record

![115_reel_reel_vinyl_record_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_reel_reel_vinyl_record_2.jpg>)

![115_reel_reel_vinyl_record.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_reel_reel_vinyl_record.jpg>)

Portable Reel to Reel

So in comes Cassettes. First came Eight-Track Cassettes

![115_eight_track_cassettes.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_eight_track_cassettes.jpg>)

, which worked good in your car. Eight different songs and then it starts over. I liked my Eight track. However, we wanted more so in come regular sized Cassette Music Players. They were in all the cars and everywhere and then came CDs and that was that. Then MP3s did to CDs what CDs did to Cassette tapes.

![115_then_mp3s_did_cds_what_cds_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_then_mp3s_did_cds_what_cds_2.jpg>)

![115_then_mp3s_did_cds_what_cds.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_then_mp3s_did_cds_what_cds.jpg>)

Eight-Track Cassette

![115_eight_track_cassette_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_eight_track_cassette_2.jpg>)

![115_eight_track_cassette.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_eight_track_cassette.jpg>)

Full Size Cassette Player

So now you younger folks know what a Cassette is.

![001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/001_applies_not_only_bible_but_shop.jpg>)

![115_will_go_just_about_anywhere.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/115_will_go_just_about_anywhere.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle

Source: http://www.dansmc.com/gearshifters.htm

GEAR SHIFTERS

![115_shift_patterns.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shift_patterns.jpg>)

![115_gear_shifters.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_gear_shifters.jpg>)

![115_shift_patterns_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shift_patterns_2.jpg>)

![115_gear_shifters_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_gear_shifters_2.jpg>)

¶ Most all current motorcycles shift with a lever operated by your left foot. With the transmission in neutral, gears are selected by pressing down for first and then letting the lever return to the center position. Then, hooking your toe under the lever, pulling up for second gear. Third and all subsequent gears are selected by pulling up on the lever after allowing it to return to the center position. Sounds complicated but it is quite easy to do. Things were not always so easy.

In the 1970s and earlier, the British made bikes that shifted with the right foot. Some were down for first and up for everything else. Some were up for first and down for the rest. Then the Japanese jumped in with neutral all the way up and everything else down, or neutral down and all the rest up. To make things really interesting they also came up with a rotary shift, which went 1,2,3,4, neutral,1,2,3,4, neutral... etc.

Supposedly, this was to make city riding easier. All you had to do was shift down one more time, to get into neutral, as you come up to a stop light. One bike, the Bridgestone 175,

![115_bridgestone_175.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_bridgestone_175.jpg>)

even gave you a choice between four gear rotary shift or five gear one up, the rest down shifting. A lever on the crankcase let you choose. Not only that, but before 1965 there was an extra neutral between fourth and fifth gears too. Some of the bikes from the 1920s and earlier even had hand shifting with a lever on the tank. I guess it's a good thing we are now somewhat standardized.

Motorcycle transmissions are made up of gears in constant mesh. Because of this, there are no syncros to speed up the gears. You don't need any. The gears are already spinning. To change between gears you need some kind of gear shifter mechanism to go along with that gear shift lever.

Gear shifters come in three different types.

Drum Shifters

Drum Slider Forks
Shaft Slider forks

Cam Plate and Shift Quadrant Shifter
Ball Lock Shifter

Drum Shifters

![115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_3.jpg>)

![115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft.jpg>)

Drum Slider Forks

![115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_4.jpg>)

![115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_2.jpg>)

Shaft Slider Forks

Drum Shifters are the most common. They come in two flavors. One type carries the shifter forks on the drum. With the other type, the forks are carried on their own shafts. Both types use grooves

![115_grooves.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_grooves.jpg>)

cut into the shifter drum, to move the forks back and forth. When the drum turns, the forks move back and forth, moving the gears in and out of engagement. These drums need something to turn them.

![115_shifter_pawl.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_pawl.jpg>)

![115_these_drums_need_something_turn_them.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_these_drums_need_something_turn_them.jpg>)

![115_shifter_pawl_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_pawl_2.jpg>)

![115_these_drums_need_something_turn_them_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_these_drums_need_something_turn_them_2.jpg>)

Most Japanese engines use a some sort of a Shift Pawl. To shift gears, you want to turn the drum only small amount and then hold it there. The shift pawl only turns the drum a set amount, each time the pawl is moved. Each time the gear shift lever is pressed down the pawl turns the drum the same amount. If the shift lever is pulled up, the pawl reverses and moves the drum in the opposite direction, the same amount. The shift lever moves the pawl and the pawl moves the drum. The drum, in turn, moves the shift forks and the shift forks move the gears in and out of mesh. The pawl presses against pins in the shift drum, but then a spring pulls the pawl back to a middle position and the drum kind of just sits there.

To keep the drum from turning, a wheel

![115_wheel.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_wheel.jpg>)

sometimes called a Shifter Detent, Shifter Drum stopper, or Shifter Cam Stopper, moves into grooves on the shifter drum, locking it into position. This wheel is spring loaded. this enables the wheel to move in and out of position, as the drum is turned by the pawl. Sometimes, instead of a wheel, a spring loaded plunder

![115_spring_loaded_plunder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_spring_loaded_plunder.jpg>)

is used. This plunger has a rounded head that fit into Shifter Cam or holes in the shifter drum. This cam, or holes, have beveled sides allowing the plunger to move smoothly in and out of the hole as the drum is turned. Like everything in motorcycles, the ratchets come in several styles.

![115_several_styles.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_several_styles.jpg>)

Check your shop manuals!

![115_pawl_adjust.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_pawl_adjust.jpg>)

![115_check_shop_manuals.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_check_shop_manuals.jpg>)

![115_pawl_adjustment.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_pawl_adjustment.jpg>)

![115_check_shop_manuals_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_check_shop_manuals_2.jpg>)

The shifter pawls on some bikes can be adjusted. To adjust simply loosen the lock nut and adjust the pawls to the center position and retighten the locknut. Usually, you will never need to adjust this. This is not exactly a high wear item! But, it can be done.

![115_ratchet_pawl.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ratchet_pawl.jpg>)

![115_but_can_done.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_but_can_done.jpg>)

![115_ratchet_pawl_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ratchet_pawl_2.jpg>)

![115_but_can_done_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_but_can_done_2.jpg>)

The shifter drum can also be turned by a Ratchet Pawl

![115_but_can_done.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_but_can_done.jpg>)

in the end of the drum. There are several styles of Ratchet Pawls depending on the manufacturer. They all work, generally, the same way. As the shifter shaft turns, one ratchet is locked out and the other ratchet turns. When the shifter shaft turns the other way, the opposite ratchet is locked out and the other ratchet turns the shaft. Check your shop manual for the exact way your shifter is set up.

Camplate and Shift Quadrant Shifter

![115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_2.jpg>)

![115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter.jpg>)

Camplate and Shift
Quadrant shifter
Mechanisms

![115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_3.jpg>)

![115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift.jpg>)

Camplate and
Shift Quadrant

![115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_4.jpg>)

![115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_2.jpg>)

Quadrant Shifter Pawl

In Camplate and Shift Quadrant shifter mechanisms, the shifter forks are carried on a plate. Grooves in this plate allow the forks to move the gears back and forth. There are twos styles of type of shifter. One has the grooves for the shifter forks cut right into the Shift Quadrant itself.

![115_shift_quadrant_itself.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shift_quadrant_itself.jpg>)

The other has the grooves machined into a Camplate

![115_camplate.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_camplate.jpg>)

that the Shift Quadrant moves. This style is used mostly on British and European Makes.

Ball Lock Shifter

![115_ball_lock_shifter_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifter_3.jpg>)

![115_ball_lock_shifter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifter.jpg>)

![115_ball_lock_shifter_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifter_4.jpg>)

![115_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg>)

Lastly, we come to Ball Lock Shifters.

![115_ball_lock_shifters.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifters.jpg>)

This shifter style was made famous by Hodaka. A few other Japanese makes used it too, but Hodaka used it exclusively in all their bikes from the 90cc to 250cc. In ball lock systems, one gear shaft has all the gears machined on the shaft. The other shaft is hollow and has four holes in each gear position. There is a ball bearing in each of these holes. A gear rides around each set of four holes. The gears have four indentions cut on the inside of the gear. A Shifter Head

![115_shifter_head.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_shifter_head.jpg>)

moves back and forth, inside the shaft. It pushes the balls out and into the indentions in each gear.

![115_ball_lock_shifter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifter.jpg>)

This changes each gear. When the next gear is chosen, the balls fall back into the shaft

![115_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/115_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg>)

releasing the gear.

Because all the gears are always engaged with each other, you do not have to use the clutch to change gears. You use the clutch in first gear to get started, but after that, just let off on the gas and shift. Nobody uses this method anymore. Probably, this is because of the high horsepower of today's motorcycle engines. There are still Hodakas out there, so you may still run into this type of shifter.

As you might expect, there are a lot of other ways to shift those gears out there but these three cover about 95% of the motorcycles you are likely to run into.

Here are some exploded views of different gear shifters for you to study.

![115_here_some_exploded_views_different_gear.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/115_here_some_exploded_views_different_gear.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/gearshifters.htm

GEAR SHIFTERS

![116_shift_patterns.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_shift_patterns.jpg>)

![116_gear_shifters.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_gear_shifters.jpg>)

![116_shift_patterns_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_shift_patterns_2.jpg>)

![116_gear_shifters_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_gear_shifters_2.jpg>)

¶ Most all current motorcycles shift with a lever operated by your left foot. With the transmission in neutral, gears are selected by pressing down for first and then letting the lever return to the center position. Then, hooking your toe under the lever, pulling up for second gear. Third and all subsequent gears are selected by pulling up on the lever after allowing it to return to the center position. Sounds complicated but it is quite easy to do. Things were not always so easy.

In the 1970s and earlier, the British made bikes that shifted with the right foot. Some were down for first and up for everything else. Some were up for first and down for the rest. Then the Japanese jumped in with neutral all the way up and everything else down, or neutral down and all the rest up. To make things really interesting they also came up with a rotary shift, which went 1,2,3,4, neutral,1,2,3,4, neutral... etc.

Supposedly, this was to make city riding easier. All you had to do was shift down one more time, to get into neutral, as you come up to a stop light. One bike, the Bridgestone 175,

![116_bridgestone_175.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_bridgestone_175.jpg>)

even gave you a choice between four gear rotary shift or five gear one up, the rest down shifting. A lever on the crankcase let you choose. Not only that, but before 1965 there was an extra neutral between fourth and fifth gears too. Some of the bikes from the 1920s and earlier even had hand shifting with a lever on the tank. I guess it's a good thing we are now somewhat standardized.

Motorcycle transmissions are made up of gears in constant mesh. Because of this, there are no syncros to speed up the gears. You don't need any. The gears are already spinning. To change between gears you need some kind of gear shifter mechanism to go along with that gear shift lever.

Gear shifters come in three different types.

Drum Shifters

Drum Slider Forks
Shaft Slider forks

Cam Plate and Shift Quadrant Shifter
Ball Lock Shifter

Drum Shifters

![116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_3.jpg>)

![116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft.jpg>)

Drum Slider Forks

![116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_4.jpg>)

![116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_drum_shifters_drum_slider_forks_shaft_2.jpg>)

Shaft Slider Forks

Drum Shifters are the most common. They come in two flavors. One type carries the shifter forks on the drum. With the other type, the forks are carried on their own shafts. Both types use grooves

![116_grooves.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_grooves.jpg>)

cut into the shifter drum, to move the forks back and forth. When the drum turns, the forks move back and forth, moving the gears in and out of engagement. These drums need something to turn them.

![116_shifter_pawl.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_shifter_pawl.jpg>)

![116_these_drums_need_something_turn_them.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_these_drums_need_something_turn_them.jpg>)

![116_shifter_pawl_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_shifter_pawl_2.jpg>)

![116_these_drums_need_something_turn_them_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_these_drums_need_something_turn_them_2.jpg>)

Most Japanese engines use a some sort of a Shift Pawl. To shift gears, you want to turn the drum only small amount and then hold it there. The shift pawl only turns the drum a set amount, each time the pawl is moved. Each time the gear shift lever is pressed down the pawl turns the drum the same amount. If the shift lever is pulled up, the pawl reverses and moves the drum in the opposite direction, the same amount. The shift lever moves the pawl and the pawl moves the drum. The drum, in turn, moves the shift forks and the shift forks move the gears in and out of mesh. The pawl presses against pins in the shift drum, but then a spring pulls the pawl back to a middle position and the drum kind of just sits there.

To keep the drum from turning, a wheel

![116_wheel.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_wheel.jpg>)

sometimes called a Shifter Detent, Shifter Drum stopper, or Shifter Cam Stopper, moves into grooves on the shifter drum, locking it into position. This wheel is spring loaded. this enables the wheel to move in and out of position, as the drum is turned by the pawl. Sometimes, instead of a wheel, a spring loaded plunder

![116_spring_loaded_plunder.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_spring_loaded_plunder.jpg>)

is used. This plunger has a rounded head that fit into Shifter Cam or holes in the shifter drum. This cam, or holes, have beveled sides allowing the plunger to move smoothly in and out of the hole as the drum is turned. Like everything in motorcycles, the ratchets come in several styles.

![116_several_styles.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_several_styles.jpg>)

Check your shop manuals!

![116_pawl_adjust.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_pawl_adjust.jpg>)

![116_check_shop_manuals.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_check_shop_manuals.jpg>)

![116_pawl_adjustment.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_pawl_adjustment.jpg>)

![116_check_shop_manuals_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_check_shop_manuals_2.jpg>)

The shifter pawls on some bikes can be adjusted. To adjust simply loosen the lock nut and adjust the pawls to the center position and retighten the locknut. Usually, you will never need to adjust this. This is not exactly a high wear item! But, it can be done.

![116_ratchet_pawl.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ratchet_pawl.jpg>)

![116_but_can_done.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_but_can_done.jpg>)

![116_ratchet_pawl_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ratchet_pawl_2.jpg>)

![116_but_can_done_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_but_can_done_2.jpg>)

The shifter drum can also be turned by a Ratchet Pawl

![116_but_can_done.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_but_can_done.jpg>)

in the end of the drum. There are several styles of Ratchet Pawls depending on the manufacturer. They all work, generally, the same way. As the shifter shaft turns, one ratchet is locked out and the other ratchet turns. When the shifter shaft turns the other way, the opposite ratchet is locked out and the other ratchet turns the shaft. Check your shop manual for the exact way your shifter is set up.

Camplate and Shift Quadrant Shifter

![116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_2.jpg>)

![116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter.jpg>)

Camplate and Shift
Quadrant shifter
Mechanisms

![116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_3.jpg>)

![116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift.jpg>)

Camplate and
Shift Quadrant

![116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_4.jpg>)

![116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate_shift_quadrant_shifter_camplate_shift_2.jpg>)

Quadrant Shifter Pawl

In Camplate and Shift Quadrant shifter mechanisms, the shifter forks are carried on a plate. Grooves in this plate allow the forks to move the gears back and forth. There are twos styles of type of shifter. One has the grooves for the shifter forks cut right into the Shift Quadrant itself.

![116_shift_quadrant_itself.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_shift_quadrant_itself.jpg>)

The other has the grooves machined into a Camplate

![116_camplate.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_camplate.jpg>)

that the Shift Quadrant moves. This style is used mostly on British and European Makes.

Ball Lock Shifter

![116_ball_lock_shifter_3.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifter_3.jpg>)

![116_ball_lock_shifter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifter.jpg>)

![116_ball_lock_shifter_4.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifter_4.jpg>)

![116_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg>)

Lastly, we come to Ball Lock Shifters.

![116_ball_lock_shifters.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifters.jpg>)

This shifter style was made famous by Hodaka. A few other Japanese makes used it too, but Hodaka used it exclusively in all their bikes from the 90cc to 250cc. In ball lock systems, one gear shaft has all the gears machined on the shaft. The other shaft is hollow and has four holes in each gear position. There is a ball bearing in each of these holes. A gear rides around each set of four holes. The gears have four indentions cut on the inside of the gear. A Shifter Head

![116_shifter_head.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_shifter_head.jpg>)

moves back and forth, inside the shaft. It pushes the balls out and into the indentions in each gear.

![116_ball_lock_shifter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifter.jpg>)

This changes each gear. When the next gear is chosen, the balls fall back into the shaft

![116_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/116_ball_lock_shifter_2.jpg>)

releasing the gear.

Because all the gears are always engaged with each other, you do not have to use the clutch to change gears. You use the clutch in first gear to get started, but after that, just let off on the gas and shift. Nobody uses this method anymore. Probably, this is because of the high horsepower of today's motorcycle engines. There are still Hodakas out there, so you may still run into this type of shifter.

As you might expect, there are a lot of other ways to shift those gears out there but these three cover about 95% of the motorcycles you are likely to run into.

Here are some exploded views of different gear shifters for you to study.

![011_check_these_things_first_check_them.gif](<01_Basics_Tools_Manuals/011_check_these_things_first_check_them.gif>)

# Dan's Motorcycle Repair "Clutches"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/clutches.htm

MANUAL CLUTCHES

![118_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_clutch.jpg>)

![118_manual_clutches.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_manual_clutches.jpg>)

¶ Clutches come in a number of designs, but they all are made to do two things.

Help the motorcycle make a smooth start from a stationary position.

Ease the transition of going from one gear to another.

Clutches are basically round baskets filled with alternating fiber and steel plates

![118_fiber_steel_plates.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_fiber_steel_plates.jpg>)

held

![118_engage_disengage_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_engage_disengage_clutch.jpg>)

![118_clutches_basically_round_baskets_filled_alternating.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_clutches_basically_round_baskets_filled_alternating.jpg>)

together, tightly, with springs. One set of plates, usually the steel ones, is connected to the transmission. The other set, usually the fiber plates, is connected to the engine. The clutch lever compresses the springs so the plates are not pressed tightly together. This allows the clutch to disengage. This works pretty well and most times clutch life is quite good. However, as the clutch wears, the plates get thinner. This lessens the spring pressure. In addition, if you slip the clutch a lot as you engage it you can burn the plates a bit. All this is not good for the clutch and sooner or later you are going to need new plates.

Most of the Japanese bikes have a wet plate clutch. This means the clutch runs in a bath of oil.
Dry plate clutches run dry with no oil. BMWs, some Harley-Davidsons, a few Japanese bikes, and others have dry clutches.

Repair is really quite simple. Remove the clutch cover, being careful to check for any washers from the kick starter that may stick to the inside of the clutch cover. Then loosen the nuts or bolts that hold and tension the clutch springs.

![118_clutch_springs.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_clutch_springs.jpg>)

Now remove the the clutch plates. On some clutches you pull the plates and the inner clutch basket as a unit

![118_unit.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_unit.jpg>)

after removing the nut or circlip

![118_circlip.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_circlip.jpg>)

holding it on.

![118_clutch_circlip.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_clutch_circlip.jpg>)

![118_circlip.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_circlip.jpg>)

On others, you remove an outer clutch plate/spring carrier and then pull out the plates individually. There may be large rubber rings or large flat spring like things between the plates. There might be only one or there could be one between every plate. Sometimes the steel plates have a sort of dished out edge on one side, for better oiling I guess. Each one is staggered from the one before it and the one after it. Be sure and put all the plates, o-rings, washers, etc. back in the same order you took them out.

Measure the thickness of the fiber plates and compare that measurement to the one given in your shop manual. If they are too thin replace them. If you do not have the thickness measurement just look at them. Most times if they are worn out they will LOOK worn out and/or smell burnt. If they smell burnt, replace them. Even if they look and measure good. Turn them on edge, both fiber and steel plates. If they are bent replace them. Look at the inner and outer fingers.

![118_inner_outer_fingers.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_inner_outer_fingers.jpg>)

If they are damaged or worn, replace them. Look at the clutch basket. Inspect the grooves

![118_grooves.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_grooves.jpg>)

the clutch plate fingers slide into. Both inner and outer. if they are badly worn, consider replacing the clutch basket.

![118_mesh_plates_together.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_mesh_plates_together.jpg>)

![118_if_they_badly_worn_consider_replacing.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_if_they_badly_worn_consider_replacing.jpg>)

Take the new fiber plates and soak them in a pan of oil for an hour or two before assembly. If you are reusing the old plates you can just coat them with oil. Make sure that the outer clutch plate that carries the springs meshes right with the clutch basket. On some, they will only go in the right way, but on others the grooves will not line up right and this prevents the springs from pushing the plates together. Some clutches will have arrows that must match. Others won't have anything... you just have to make sure they mesh up right.

Most clutches have the disengagement mechanism in the center of the clutch.

![118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center_2.jpg>)

![118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg>)

Some activate it from the clutch cover

![118_clutches_basically_round_baskets_filled_alternating.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_clutches_basically_round_baskets_filled_alternating.jpg>)

and some use a rod

![118_some_activate_clutch_cover_some_use.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_some_activate_clutch_cover_some_use.jpg>)

going through the mainshaft of the transmission. This rod is activated by a cam or worm

![118_cam_worm.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_cam_worm.jpg>)

on one end of the rod, pushing the rod against the spring plate, releasing the clutch. This rod passes in front of the counter shaft sprocket and can easily be bent by small twigs and branches and gook thrown off by the rear chain. If you have this type and your clutch suddenly stops working, check here first for a bent clutch rod

![118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg>)

, before you tear the clutch apart. These rods can also be in two parts

![118_two_parts.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_two_parts.jpg>)

with a ball bearing between them. Some have a ball bearing only on the worm end. Don't let that ball bearing fall out and get lost.

![118_stuck_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_stuck_clutch.jpg>)

![118_don_t_let_ball_bearing_fall.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_don_t_let_ball_bearing_fall.jpg>)

Sometimes, when a bike has been sitting a long time, like over winter, the clutch plates will stick together. You pull the clutch lever in but the plates will not disengage. About 60-70% of the time you can get them to release by running the bike up to 15-20 MPH and locking up the rear brake while you hold the clutch lever in (disengaged). If this does not break it loose, you will have to take the clutch cover off and with the lever held on, pry the plates apart with a screwdriver and reoil them a bit.

Remember, most engines have a flat metal shim on the kick starter shaft. Lots of times it will stick to the clutch cover when you pull it off. Make sure you put it back on the kick starter.

After everything is finished and the clutch cover back on, don't forget to refill the engine with oil.

Some clutches, like the BMWs, Norton Commandos and some Harleys, have a single (or two) Heavy spring that is held in by a large circlip. These require a special tool to remove.

The BSAs and Triumphs require a special puller to get the clutch basket off.

All clutches must have a bit of free play in the cables and rods so the clutch springs can exert the maximum amount of pressure on the plates. If there is an adjustment screw

![118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg>)

on the rod, loosen the lock nut and tighten the screw until there is no more free play, then loosen it about 1/8 of a turn and tighten the lock nut. The adjustment screw can be right OR left thread, so watch out. A shop manual would be of help here. The adjusting screw can also be UNDER the clutch cover on the clutch spring plate. After you have made this adjustment, adjust the clutch cable keeping at least a little free play in the cable. Remember, on some bikes, the only adjustment is the free play of the clutch cable.

![118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/118_most_clutches_have_disengagement_mechanism_center.jpg>)

Depending on the bike, the cable can be adjusted on both ends and in the center somewhere, only on both ends or only on one end.

# Dan's Motorcycle "Automatic Clutches"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/autoclutch.htm

AUTOMATIC DRIVES & CLUTCHES

![120_shoe_type_automatic_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_shoe_type_automatic_clutch.jpg>)

![120_automatic_drives_clutches.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_automatic_drives_clutches.jpg>)

¶ Automatic Drives and Clutches on motorcycles have been around a long time. The Rudge Multi

![120_rudge_multi.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_rudge_multi.jpg>)

used a form of the variable pulley drive

![120_variable_pulley_drive.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_variable_pulley_drive.jpg>)

, back in the 1912, to give a supposed 19 speeds. Most of the automatic clutches you will run across will be one of four types.

Centrifugal with clutch plates.
Centrifugal with clutch shoes
Centrifugal drive and driven clutches with a belt connecting them. (Snowmobile Type)
Fluid Torque converter

Centrifugal with Clutch Plates

![120_plate_auto_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_plate_auto_clutch.jpg>)

![120_snowmobile_type_fluid_torque_converter_centrifugal.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_snowmobile_type_fluid_torque_converter_centrifugal.jpg>)

This type has clutch plates and usually goes with a transmission. Weights press the steel and fiber plates together engaging the clutch as the engine speed rises. Weak springs disengage the clutch as engine speed drops. Honda 50, 70 and 90cc engines and others, use this type of clutch. These Hondas use a lever

![120_lever.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_lever.jpg>)

on the end of the shifter shaft to completely disengage the clutch to shift gears.

Centrifugal with Clutch Shoes

![120_shoe_auto_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_shoe_auto_clutch.jpg>)

![120_centrifugal_clutch_shoes.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_centrifugal_clutch_shoes.jpg>)

This type has clutch shoes

![120_automatic_drives_clutches.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_automatic_drives_clutches.jpg>)

. The shoes are held in with springs. As the engine speed rises, the shoes press against the clutch housing, and engages the clutch. These are used a lot on 4 wheel ATVs along with a regular clutch and transmission. Go carts and those little, big wheeled, mini-bikes with Briggs & Stratton engines also use this type of clutch.

![120_clutch.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/120_clutch.gif>)

Centrifugal Drive and Driven Belt Clutch

This type has a drive clutch and a driven clutch that are connected by a big thick belt. The sides of the drive clutch

![120_drive_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_drive_clutch.jpg>)

(mounted on the engine crankshaft) are pressed together with weights as the engine speed goes up. This makes the belt climb the sides effectively making the front pulley bigger. The driven clutch

![120_driven_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_driven_clutch.jpg>)

(Mounted on what ends up being the countershaft sprocket) has a weak spring that pushes the pulley sides together. As the front pulley gets bigger the belt pushes against the rear pulley, overcoming the spring, and making the rear pulley smaller. What all this means is that you have a infinitely variable transmission with this type of automatic clutch.

![120_automatic_clutch.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_automatic_clutch.jpg>)

This type is used on Honda Odyssey 4 wheelers and lots and lots of snowmobiles. It is also used on some mini-bikes, go-carts, and on Rokon two wheel drive dirt bikes. The old Rokon 340cc motorcycles

![120_rokon_340cc_motorcycles.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_rokon_340cc_motorcycles.jpg>)

used it too.

Fluid Torque Converters

Honda had a 750cc and a 400cc, Suzuki had a 450cc, and Moto Guzzi had a 1000cc automatic.
Most were made in the late 70's, early 80's and had a 2-speed gear box with a Fluid Torque Converter

![120_fluid_torque_converter.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/120_fluid_torque_converter.jpg>)

that worked just like a car. You don't see too many of these bikes nowadays, and on most, the Torque Converter was a sealed unit, requiring no service.

Repair

Repair on all of these is pretty simple. If the plates, shoes or belts are badly worn replace them.

# Dan's Motorcycle "Counter Balancers"

Source: https://www.dansmc.com/counterbalancers.htm

MOTORCYCLE COUNTER BALANCERS

![122_motorcycle_counter_balancers.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_motorcycle_counter_balancers.jpg>)

![122_motorcycle_counter_balancers.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_motorcycle_counter_balancers.jpg>)

A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Proverbs 11:1

¶ Most motorcycle engines vibrate. Some more then others. Some bike engines are smooth, I'll grant you that. I have, personally, balanced a nickel, on the cylinder head of a Honda GL1000, with the engine running 5000 RPM. Smooth is out there, but not every engine is a flat four. The reason the flat, four cylinder engine is so smooth is because the opposing pistons move in and out together. This cancels out the vibration from the opposite cylinder.

On a single cylinder engine, The vibration from the weight of the moving piston is canceled out, in part, by the engines flywheel weight. If the engine has more then one cylinder, there are more whirling masses of metal. This makes things easier to balance. A twin is going to be a bit smoother then a single. A three cylinder engine is going to be a lot smoother and a four smoother still.

Engines with three, four and six cylinders usually do not have Balancers, but some four cylinder machines, like the Yamaha Venture

![122_yamaha_venture.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_yamaha_venture.jpg>)

, do have a balancer. Most fours do not. For most singles and twins, we need a Counter Balancer. A single cylinder engine normally has one Counter Balancer and it works like this

![122_motorcycle_counter_balancers.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_motorcycle_counter_balancers.jpg>)

:

At "Top Dead Center" (TDC) the upward forces of the piston and connecting rod weight (100%) is off set by the downward flywheel weight (50%) and the Counter Balancer weight (50%). The total imbalance now equals zero.
At 90 degrees after TDC the forces of the piston and connecting rod is zero. The crankshaft and balancer weights off set each other so they are zero too.
At "Bottom Dead Center" (BDC) the piston and Counter Balancer weights again oppose each other canceling the inertia of their weights out.
At 90 degrees "Before Top Dead Center" (BTDC) the weights again cancel each other out.

Twin cylinder engines usually have two Counter Balancers and work in a similar manner as singles cylinder engines.

The balance factor of the crankshaft flywheel weights is changed to match the weight of the Counter balance. Do not remove the Counter Balancer(s) from your engine to get more horse power unless you rebalance the crankshaft flywheel weights.

Counter Balancers come in two types of drives.

Gear Drive
Chain Drive

There can be one or two balancers. I suppose you could have more but I've never seen more then two on one engine. They seem to work pretty good. They can turn a ride that causes you to stop every half hour and scratch all over, to a ride that is quite pleasant.

![122_they_can_turn_ride_causes_stop_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_they_can_turn_ride_causes_stop_2.jpg>)

![122_they_can_turn_ride_causes_stop.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_they_can_turn_ride_causes_stop.jpg>)

Gear Drive Counterbalancer

![122_gear_drive_counterbalancer_2.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_gear_drive_counterbalancer_2.jpg>)

![122_gear_drive_counterbalancer.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_gear_drive_counterbalancer.jpg>)

Chain Drive Counterbalancer

![122_gear_alignment.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_gear_alignment.jpg>)

![122_gear_drive_counterbalancer_chain_drive_counterbalancer.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_gear_drive_counterbalancer_chain_drive_counterbalancer.jpg>)

Gear drive Counterbalancers do not change or go out of adjustment, but they must be set right when you assemble the engine. There will be a gear on the crankshaft and it will mesh with the gear on the balabcer's shaft. There are punch marks on both gears and they must align. Double check those marks. You will not believe how much it vibrates if they are a couple teeth off. I did that once, on purpose of course. (Yeah, right,... sure.) It made that bike a definite tooth rattler. Changed it back to the right setting... smooth as silk. The gears can be outside the crankcase, under the clutch cover, or inside the crankcase. In other words, an easy goof to fix, or a very hard one. Word to the wise, double check your work. A lot of Honda, Yamaha and Suzuki singles use this type of Counter Balancer.

Chain Drive Counterbalancers can change as the chain wears. They usually have a way to take up or adjust slack on the chain as it wears. Some Yamaha and Honda twins use adjustable, chain driven, Balancers. Usually, one of the sprockets can move, tightening or loosening the chain. Sometimes the adjuster sprocket is spring loaded. Simply loosen and then tighten the adjuster, and the Balancer chain will be adjusted automatically, at least till the chain is worn out.

![122_chain_alignment.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_chain_alignment.jpg>)

![122_simply_loosen_then_tighten_adjuster_balancer.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_simply_loosen_then_tighten_adjuster_balancer.jpg>)

The drive and driven sprockets will have a mark on the sprocket and a mark on the crankcase. There will be one or two idler and/or adjustment sprockets too, depending on the number of Balancers used. The marks on the dive and driven sprockets must match the corresponding marks on the crankcase with the chain assembled and everything hooked up and the chain adjusted. If the sprockets are fitted on the Balancer shaft with a spline, the shaft will have a punch mark

![122_punch_mark.jpg](<06_Engine_Parts/122_punch_mark.jpg>)

on it too. This mark must be matched to the mark on the sprocket.

Kawasaki 400/440 twins use two, chain driven, Balancers that are not adjustable. When you assemble the engine, match the plated links of the Balancer chain with the mark on each Balancer sprocket. When the chain wears, you must replace it. This entails splitting the crankcases. This may not be as bad as it sounds. I've seen a number of these engines go 30-40,000 miles before problems arise.

Counter Balancers are a good way to smooth out the vibes on single and twin cylinder engines. They must be installed right and if it's got a chain, it must be adjusted right, and remember, chains do wear out.

![122_they_must_installed_right_if_s.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/122_they_must_installed_right_if_s.gif>)

![122_they_must_installed_right_if_s.gif](<06_Engine_Parts/122_they_must_installed_right_if_s.gif>)
